messages.content: I want to design asynchronous distributed checkpointing for training. The goal is to preserve recoverable training-state consistency across worker failures and changes in model parallelism. In particular, recovery after any single-worker crash must use a committed, globally consistent model, optimizer, and RNG state. Restores also need to work across tensor-parallel layouts, while checkpoint-induced throughput loss stays at or below 5% versus checkpoint-free training.

That sets three linked requirements for the design. A recoverable checkpoint must represent one globally consistent training state, including model parameters, optimizer state, and RNG state. A crash of any one worker must not force recovery from an incomplete or inconsistent state. The saved state must also be restorable under a different tensor-parallel layout, and the cost of checkpointing during training must limit throughput loss to 5% relative to checkpoint-free training. These are design targets, not results already demonstrated.
What does “globally consistent” add beyond having each worker save its own state?

Separate worker saves are not enough if they cannot be understood as parts of the same recoverable training state. “Globally consistent” means the model, optimizer, and RNG portions used for recovery agree with one another across the distributed workers. Recovery should not assemble a model from one logical point in training with optimizer or RNG state from an incompatible point. The requirement concerns the state that can actually be restored, not merely whether each worker produced a file.
And why emphasize that the state is committed?

Commitment distinguishes a checkpoint that is eligible for recovery from checkpoint work that is still in progress. Asynchronous saving can leave some portions available before the complete distributed state is ready. The requirement is to recover a committed, globally consistent state, rather than treating an unfinished collection of portions as a valid checkpoint. It does not specify a particular commit mechanism or storage format.
Suppose a worker crashes while checkpointing is underway. Does the wording cover that case?

Yes: “after any single-worker crash” does not exclude a crash during checkpoint activity. Recovery still needs a committed, globally consistent model, optimizer, and RNG state. Work in progress at the moment of the crash cannot be assumed recoverable merely because some of it was saved. The goal does not say that every in-progress checkpoint must finish after a crash, or that no training work can be lost since the most recent committed checkpoint.
Does asynchronous mean training can never pause to coordinate a checkpoint?

Not necessarily. Asynchronous describes the intended checkpointing approach; it does not, by itself, prohibit every moment of coordination. The important distinction is that allowing checkpoint work to proceed asynchronously cannot weaken the recovery guarantee. Any coordination or background work in a proposed design would also have to fit the throughput target, but the goal does not prescribe how to arrange it.
Why name the optimizer state separately from the model?

Because restoring model parameters alone does not necessarily restore the corresponding training state. The optimizer state is part of what must be recovered, and it must be consistent with the recovered model state. The requirement is about resuming from a coherent training state, not only loading model weights that happen to be available.
RNG state seems easy to overlook. Is it equally part of the recovery guarantee?

Yes. RNG state is explicitly included alongside model and optimizer state. A checkpoint that recovers those first two components but omits RNG state would not meet the stated requirement. The goal calls for a globally consistent recovered RNG state; it does not, without further specification, define a particular RNG organization or promise that every downstream event will be identical under every tensor-parallel layout.
How should I interpret restores across tensor-parallel layouts?

A checkpoint must remain usable when the tensor-parallel layout at restore differs from the layout under which the state was checkpointed. In conceptual terms, the recoverable training state cannot depend on restoring the exact same partitioning of tensors across workers. That portability applies to the checkpoint as a training state, including the required model, optimizer, and RNG components. The goal does not choose a representation or a repartitioning method.
So could I satisfy portability by loading just the model under a new layout?

No. Loading the model alone would address only part of the stated goal. Restores across tensor-parallel layouts must still respect the recovery requirement for a committed, globally consistent model, optimizer, and RNG state. The changed layout should not turn the checkpoint into a model-only restore or make its optimizer and RNG state inconsistent with the recovered model.
Is the layout change itself required after every worker failure?

No such sequence is specified. The goal requires recovery after any single-worker crash and support for restores across tensor-parallel layouts. Those requirements must coexist in the design, but the wording does not say that every crash triggers a layout change. Nor does it limit layout portability to cases where a crash has occurred.
Can you put the 5% performance condition in precise comparative terms?

The reference is checkpoint-free training throughput. Checkpoint-induced throughput loss must be no more than 5% relative to that reference; equivalently, checkpointed training throughput should be at least 95% of checkpoint-free training throughput under a like-for-like comparison. This is a throughput comparison, not a statement that checkpoint operations may occupy exactly 5% of wall-clock time. The goal supplies no measured throughput values.
Does being asynchronous establish that the 5% threshold will be met?

No. Asynchronous checkpointing is the kind of design requested, while the 5% bound is an additional performance constraint. An asynchronous design could still impose enough work or coordination to exceed that loss. Likewise, meeting a throughput figure would not excuse recovery from an inconsistent checkpoint. Both the recovery properties and the comparative throughput bound have to hold.
What exactly does “any single-worker crash” commit us to, and what does it leave open?

It means the recovery guarantee must not depend on which one worker crashes. Following such a crash, recovery must be possible from a committed, globally consistent model, optimizer, and RNG state. It does not expressly require tolerance of multiple simultaneous worker crashes, recovery of uncommitted checkpoint work, or resumption from the exact moment of failure. Those would be additional requirements rather than implications of this one.
Could we describe this as keeping checkpoint capture off the critical path, without specifying how?

You can describe minimizing disruption to training as the performance intent behind asynchronous checkpointing. I would avoid turning “off the critical path” into an absolute guarantee, since the stated constraint is specifically a throughput loss of no more than 5% versus checkpoint-free training. The goal leaves room for design choices about capture and coordination, provided the committed-state recovery, layout portability, and throughput requirements are all met.
Then the checkpoint should be thought of as a recoverable training state, rather than a set of unrelated worker artifacts?

Exactly as a statement of the design goal. Whatever artifacts a design might produce, the unit eligible for recovery has to represent a committed, globally consistent model, optimizer, and RNG state. It must withstand any single-worker crash, remain restorable across tensor-parallel layouts, and do so with checkpoint-induced throughput loss limited to 5% relative to checkpoint-free training. The particular mechanism for achieving those properties remains open.

How about this as the checkpointing approach: take step-aligned copy-on-write snapshots of the model, optimizer, and logical RNG state, asynchronously upload globally indexed shards, and atomically commit a manifest only after those uploads?

That is a concrete proposal for the goal we discussed. Step alignment identifies one logical training step for the model, optimizer, and RNG snapshots. Copy-on-write aims to keep that captured state stable while training continues; asynchronous uploads move the shards without requiring the entire upload to finish before training proceeds. The globally indexed shards are intended to remain interpretable across tensor-parallel layouts, and the atomic manifest commit marks when the complete checkpoint becomes eligible for recovery. These are proposed design properties, not evidence yet that the recovery or 5% throughput targets have been achieved.
Can we unpack “step-aligned”? Is it just a timestamp attached to each worker’s data?

It means more than attaching matching labels. The model, optimizer, and logical RNG snapshots are meant to represent the same logical training step, so a restore does not combine components from incompatible points in training. A label could describe that alignment, but a label alone would not establish that the captured contents actually agree. The proposal does not specify the coordination procedure used to obtain the aligned snapshots.
If one worker starts copying later than another, does that necessarily break the proposal?

Not necessarily. The important property is the logical step represented by each captured component, not whether every physical copy operation starts at the same instant. Copy-on-write is proposed to preserve a captured view while later training activity may continue. Whether a particular implementation successfully produces step-aligned views across workers would still need to be established; the proposal does not define its timing details.
What work is copy-on-write doing here?

Conceptually, it separates the state selected for a checkpoint from subsequent changes made by training. That lets an asynchronous upload read a stable snapshot rather than a mixture of older and newer values. In this proposal, that applies to the model, optimizer, and logical RNG snapshots. Copy-on-write is a proposed way to preserve the selected view, not a guarantee by itself that all distributed components were selected at the same logical step.
Does saying copy-on-write commit us to a particular memory layout or copying schedule?

No. It names the snapshotting approach, but the node does not prescribe a specific layout, when individual bytes are copied, or how much additional memory is used. Those details matter to an eventual implementation and to its throughput, yet they are not decisions contained in this proposal.
Why call it a logical RNG snapshot instead of simply saying RNG bytes?

The word “logical” emphasizes RNG state as part of the recoverable training state, rather than identifying it solely with the worker that happened to hold it when the snapshot was taken. That framing matters when a restore may use a different tensor-parallel layout. It does not specify an RNG representation, a mapping between layouts, or a guarantee of identical future random draws across different layouts.
I want to be careful not to imply that the model snapshot alone defines the step.

Right. The proposal explicitly names model, optimizer, and logical RNG snapshots as step-aligned. The optimizer and RNG portions must correspond to the selected model state, rather than being treated as optional attachments collected whenever convenient. That is how this proposal addresses the goal of recovering a globally consistent training state.
Where do the globally indexed shards fit into that picture?

They are the units proposed for asynchronous upload after the snapshots are taken. “Globally indexed” suggests identifying their place in the checkpointed state in a way that is meaningful beyond a particular worker’s local tensor-parallel assignment. That supports the intended restore across layouts. The proposal does not specify a shard size, an index format, or a concrete repartitioning algorithm.
Would worker-numbered files be enough to count as globally indexed?

A worker number by itself describes where something was held, not necessarily what portion of the overall recoverable state it represents. The point of global indexing is to make shard identity interpretable as part of the checkpoint even if the tensor-parallel layout changes. The proposal does not rule on any specific naming scheme; it states the property the shard identification is meant to provide.
What is the ordering between upload and commit?

The proposed ordering is explicit: asynchronously upload the globally indexed shards before the atomic manifest commit. The commit is the point at which the checkpoint is presented as a complete, recoverable unit. Shards that have been uploaded while the manifest is not committed are still checkpoint work in progress, not by themselves a committed global training state.
Why make the manifest commit atomic?

Atomicity is meant to avoid exposing a half-committed checkpoint as recoverable. The manifest either becomes committed as a unit or does not; recovery should not have to interpret a partially committed manifest as though it described a complete model, optimizer, and logical RNG snapshot. The proposal does not name a particular atomic-write or transaction mechanism.
Does an atomic manifest automatically make all the shard data safe?

No. The sequencing in the proposal puts shard upload before commit, and the recovery goal requires a committed state whose needed contents can actually be recovered. Atomicity of the manifest addresses the visibility of commitment; it does not, on its own, prove that every referenced shard is available or that the snapshots were consistent. Those properties would have to hold for the design to satisfy the goal.
Say a single worker crashes before the manifest is committed. What would this proposal let recovery use?

The in-progress checkpoint would not yet be committed, even if some globally indexed shards had finished uploading. Recovery would need a committed, globally consistent model, optimizer, and RNG state; the proposal does not claim that the unfinished upload is usable as one. It also does not say how much training progress lies between a crash and the most recent committed checkpoint.
And if the worker crashes after the atomic commit?

The intent is that the committed manifest identifies a complete checkpoint assembled from the uploaded, globally indexed shards, so recovery can use the corresponding step-aligned model, optimizer, and logical RNG state. That describes the proposed recovery boundary, not a demonstrated crash test. The requirement remains recovery after any single-worker crash, regardless of which worker it is.
Is an asynchronous upload compatible with a single atomic commit?

Yes, conceptually. The shard transfers can take place asynchronously, while the manifest commit is a distinct event that occurs afterward. Asynchrony of the uploads does not require partial commitment, and an atomic commit does not mean all uploads had to occur simultaneously. The proposal leaves the exact coordination of that transition unspecified.
If the upload takes time, can training continue changing the model while the shards are being uploaded?

That is the purpose of pairing asynchronous upload with copy-on-write snapshots. Training may continue to change its active state while the upload reads the selected, stable snapshot. The checkpoint still has to represent the step-aligned model, optimizer, and logical RNG state captured for it; uploading later must not quietly substitute newer values. How well this separation performs is not established by the proposal alone.
Could the globally indexed shards be viewed as the way to avoid binding the checkpoint to its original tensor-parallel layout?

That is the intended role. If shard identities express their position in the overall checkpointed state rather than only their original worker placement, a restore under another tensor-parallel layout can, in principle, interpret the saved pieces. The proposal still does not spell out how model, optimizer, and logical RNG state are reconstructed in a new layout, so cross-layout restore remains a requirement the design must satisfy, not an outcome to assume.
Does the manifest commit also have to say which training step the pieces represent?

The proposed checkpoint must make its step-aligned pieces interpretable together; otherwise commitment would not establish a coherent recoverable state. The node does not prescribe the manifest’s fields or encoding, however. What matters here is that the atomic commit identifies a complete set of uploaded, globally indexed shards for the selected training-state snapshot.
I’m wary of treating the manifest as a substitute for consistency.

That caution is appropriate. An atomic manifest can define when a checkpoint becomes visible as committed, but it cannot retroactively align mismatched model, optimizer, and RNG contents. Step-aligned snapshots address the content of the state; copy-on-write protects that captured content during asynchronous work; upload supplies its shards; and atomic manifest commit defines the recoverable boundary. Each part serves a different aspect of the proposal.
What should we say about the 5% throughput-loss limit at this stage?

It remains a constraint on the proposed design: checkpoint-induced throughput loss must be at most 5% versus checkpoint-free training. Copy-on-write capture and asynchronous shard upload are proposed ways to limit disruption, but they can themselves impose costs. No measurements are supplied, so we cannot say this approach meets the 5% limit merely because its uploads are asynchronous.
So a design could get the commit and crash behavior right but still fall short?

Yes. Recovering a committed, globally consistent model, optimizer, and RNG state after any single-worker crash is necessary, but the goal also requires restores across tensor-parallel layouts and no more than 5% checkpoint-induced throughput loss relative to checkpoint-free training. The proposed snapshot, shard, and manifest structure is meant to address these requirements together; it is not itself proof that every requirement has been met.
How concise can we make the proposal without losing its important ordering?

One concise formulation is: capture step-aligned copy-on-write snapshots of the model, optimizer, and logical RNG state; asynchronously upload their globally indexed shards; then atomically commit the manifest. Keeping “upload” before “commit” is important, as is keeping all three state components within the step-aligned snapshot. The recovery and throughput requirements remain the criteria against which that proposal would be judged.
Can step-boundary copy-on-write capture align optimizer and RNG versions across ranks without exceeding 5% throughput loss?

It could in principle, but neither step-boundary capture nor copy-on-write alone establishes both outcomes. The consistency question is whether every rank’s captured optimizer and logical RNG state belongs to the same selected training step and agrees with the captured model state. The performance question is separate: whether taking and preserving those snapshots, along with the rest of checkpointing, reduces throughput by no more than 5% relative to checkpoint-free training. The proposal gives an approach to evaluate, not a measured answer.
Does choosing a step boundary give us alignment automatically?

It gives a meaningful point at which to define alignment, but it does not automatically prove that every captured component reflects that point. A step-boundary snapshot would need to represent the intended optimizer and RNG versions on every rank, rather than a mixture of states associated with different steps. Calling all the snapshots by the same step name would not be enough if their contents differed in that way.
What do you mean by an optimizer or RNG “version” here?

Here, “version” means the state associated with the chosen logical training step, not a particular file-versioning scheme. The question is whether each rank’s optimizer snapshot and logical RNG snapshot correspond to that same step and to the model snapshot. The supplied proposal does not define a specific version identifier or how one would be recorded.
So I shouldn’t think of it as merely taking three independent snapshots near the same time?

Right. Temporal proximity is not the same as a globally consistent training state. The snapshots need to be step-aligned across ranks and across the model, optimizer, and logical RNG components. Copy-on-write can help preserve a selected view once captured, but it cannot make independently selected, incompatible views consistent after the fact.
Where exactly is copy-on-write helpful for this question?

Its proposed role is to keep the selected state stable while training proceeds and checkpoint work continues asynchronously. If the state selected at the step boundary is coherent, copy-on-write can help prevent later modifications from changing what the checkpoint reads. It addresses preservation of the captured versions; it does not by itself decide whether the versions were aligned across ranks at capture time.
Could we say the capture must agree on a single logical step, rather than requiring every rank to do its copying at the same instant?

Yes, that expresses the consistency requirement without imposing a particular physical timing rule. What matters is that the recoverable contents correspond to one logical training step across ranks, including optimizer and logical RNG state. Different physical capture timings would be acceptable only if they still produce that coherent view. The question does not specify how to ensure this.
Why focus on optimizer and RNG versions when the model is also in the snapshot?

The model is part of the same required state, but optimizer and RNG state make the alignment question explicit. A model snapshot would not be enough if its accompanying optimizer or RNG snapshots reflected a different logical step on some ranks. All three components must fit together for recovery to use a committed, globally consistent training state.
Would an atomic manifest commit resolve a version mismatch discovered at the step boundary?

No. Atomic commit controls whether a checkpoint becomes visible as committed; it does not change the contents captured on the ranks. If optimizer or RNG snapshots do not align, committing a manifest cannot make them align. The proposed sequence depends on capturing a coherent state before treating the uploaded shards as a recoverable checkpoint.
Could the asynchronous upload be fast enough that capture overhead doesn’t matter?

That cannot be inferred from the proposal. Uploading asynchronously may reduce the time training spends waiting for uploads, but step-boundary capture and preservation of copy-on-write snapshots may still affect throughput. The relevant limit is the checkpoint-induced throughput loss of the design as a whole, not just the duration of a particular upload or capture operation.
Is the 5% bound a cap on how long ranks can spend at the step boundary?

No. It is a comparison of training throughput with checkpointing against checkpoint-free training: the induced loss must be no more than 5%. Time spent at a step boundary could contribute to that loss, but the bound is not stated as a per-boundary time allowance. Other checkpoint-related work can also affect the throughput comparison.
If the capture itself is consistent, can we answer yes to the question?

That would address the alignment half, assuming the captured model, optimizer, and logical RNG states truly correspond across ranks. It would not establish the throughput half. Answering yes to the full question would require both that consistency property and throughput loss at or below 5% versus checkpoint-free training.
Conversely, if throughput loss is under 5%, can we tolerate occasional misaligned RNG state?

No. Performance does not relax the recovery requirement. The checkpoint must permit recovery of a committed, globally consistent model, optimizer, and RNG state after any single-worker crash. A fast capture that sometimes commits incompatible RNG or optimizer versions would not satisfy that requirement.
What would count as a useful consistency check in discussing this, without choosing an implementation?

At a conceptual level, ask whether each component of the candidate checkpoint can be attributed to the same selected logical step on every rank, and whether recovery would reconstruct those components together. That frames the property to establish without prescribing a synchronization method, metadata format, or test result. The same check must apply to optimizer and logical RNG state, not just the model.
Would checking that the manifest refers to every uploaded shard be the same check?

It is related but not the same. A complete set of referenced shards addresses whether the committed checkpoint includes its intended pieces. Version alignment asks whether the contents of those pieces represent a mutually consistent training step. A checkpoint could be complete in one sense and still contain mismatched optimizer or RNG versions; neither condition substitutes for the other.
How should we frame the performance side without implying we’ve run a benchmark?

State it as a criterion to establish: compare throughput under this checkpointing approach with checkpoint-free training under a like-for-like comparison, and determine whether checkpoint-induced loss is at most 5%. We can discuss potential sources of overhead in general terms, but no throughput measurements are provided, so the threshold has not been demonstrated here.
Does changing tensor-parallel layout alter the immediate question?

The immediate question is whether step-boundary copy-on-write capture can align optimizer and RNG versions across ranks within the 5% throughput-loss limit. The broader design still needs restores across tensor-parallel layouts, so a coherent snapshot must remain usable as a recoverable training state under that requirement. But layout portability does not answer whether capture was aligned or whether its throughput cost meets the bound.
Then what is the most careful answer to my original question?

Step-boundary copy-on-write capture is a plausible way to select and preserve aligned model, optimizer, and logical RNG state across ranks while checkpoint work proceeds asynchronously. It can meet the stated goal only if the selected versions actually form one globally consistent training state and checkpoint-induced throughput loss is no more than 5% versus checkpoint-free training. The information here does not establish either property for a particular implementation, so the answer remains conditional.

Here is a hypothesis for the capture question: at 1,000-step intervals, a post-update rank barrier plus copy-on-write capture preserves identical state step IDs across ranks with no more than 5% throughput loss.

That is a testable hypothesis, not an established result. It proposes a checkpoint-capture cadence of every 1,000 steps, with ranks reaching a barrier after the update and then using copy-on-write capture. The expected consistency property is identical state step IDs across ranks; the expected performance property is checkpoint-induced throughput loss of at most 5% relative to checkpoint-free training.
What is the significance of placing the barrier after the update?

The hypothesis uses the completed update as the reference for the state being captured. A post-update rank barrier is intended to bring ranks to the same step boundary before copy-on-write capture preserves their views. That is the proposed reason it might yield identical state step IDs; the wording does not itself demonstrate that the model, optimizer, and logical RNG contents are coherent.
Does the barrier mean every rank’s tensors and RNG values should be numerically identical?

No. The hypothesis says the *state step IDs* are identical across ranks. It does not say that every rank holds identical tensor values or identical RNG values. For a distributed training state, the important question is whether each rank’s captured portion belongs to the same logical step and fits the overall recoverable state.
I’m especially concerned about optimizer and RNG versions. Does an identical step ID settle that?

It would be a useful alignment property, but an identical ID alone would not settle the content question. To address the earlier capture question, the optimizer and logical RNG snapshots would have to actually correspond to the identified post-update step, along with the model snapshot. The hypothesis predicts aligned IDs; it has not shown that the captured contents match those IDs.
Why pair a rank barrier with copy-on-write rather than treating the barrier as the snapshot?

They play different conceptual roles. The post-update barrier is proposed as a way for ranks to agree on the step boundary. Copy-on-write capture is proposed to preserve the state selected at that boundary while later training activity and asynchronous checkpoint work proceed. Reaching the barrier does not, by itself, preserve the selected state for a later upload.
And copy-on-write on its own would not make ranks agree on a step ID?

Correct. Copy-on-write can preserve whatever view was selected, but it does not independently establish that different ranks selected the same logical step. The hypothesis combines it with a post-update rank barrier for that reason. Whether the combination delivers identical state step IDs remains the claim to evaluate.
Is every 1,000 steps a measurement we have already found to work?

No. The 1,000-step interval is part of the hypothesis. It specifies how frequently this barrier-and-capture operation would occur, not an observed optimal cadence or a demonstrated throughput result. The same applies to the ≤5% figure: it is the proposed bound to meet, not a reported measurement.
Does the hypothesis say that the barrier happens continuously during the 1,000 steps?

No. It places the proposed post-update rank barrier and copy-on-write capture at 1,000-step intervals. It does not describe what happens at every intervening step, or prescribe any additional barrier schedule. Reading it as a continuous barrier would add a condition that is not stated.
Could we call the 5% number a cap on the cost of the barrier?

That would be too narrow. The hypothesis is about throughput loss for the checkpointing approach, compared with checkpoint-free training. The barrier may contribute to that loss, but copy-on-write capture and other checkpoint-related work may contribute too. A barrier that appears inexpensive in isolation would not establish that total checkpoint-induced throughput loss is ≤5%.
Does using a barrier conflict with calling the checkpointing design asynchronous?

Not necessarily. This hypothesis permits coordination at the post-update capture boundary while the proposed shard upload remains asynchronous. “Asynchronous” need not mean that every part of capture occurs without coordination. The performance condition is what constrains the overall disruption: throughput loss must be no more than 5% relative to checkpoint-free training.
How precise is “identical state step IDs”? Are we claiming that every component is captured at exactly the same physical instant?

No. Identical state step IDs express agreement on the logical step represented by the captured state across ranks. Physical copying need not occur at an identical instant if the resulting model, optimizer, and logical RNG snapshots still represent that same step. The hypothesis does not specify the physical timing of individual copies.
Could identical IDs still mask one rank’s RNG snapshot belonging to a different step?

Yes, if an ID were attached without the corresponding content actually reflecting that step. That distinction is why the hypothesis should not be presented as proof of global consistency. The substantive alignment question remains whether each captured model, optimizer, and logical RNG portion represents the stated step, not merely whether the portions carry matching IDs.
If the IDs do align, have we also solved recovery after any single-worker crash?

Not on that basis alone. This hypothesis concerns capture alignment and throughput at 1,000-step intervals. The broader design also requires an uploaded, committed checkpoint from which a globally consistent model, optimizer, and RNG state can be recovered after any single-worker crash. Matching state step IDs would support that goal, but would not by itself establish shard availability or a committed manifest.
What about a restore under another tensor-parallel layout?

The hypothesis does not resolve that requirement either. A shared logical step across ranks is relevant to producing a coherent checkpoint, but restoring it under a different tensor-parallel layout also depends on the proposed globally indexed shards being usable for that restore. We should not infer layout portability merely from the barrier, the interval, or the matching state step IDs.
Would failure to meet either predicted property defeat this particular hypothesis?

Yes. As stated, it predicts both identical state step IDs across ranks and throughput loss of no more than 5%. Observing one without the other would not support the combined claim. For example, matching IDs would not answer the performance question, and low throughput loss would not answer the alignment question.
Can we explain the expected benefit of the 1,000-step spacing without asserting an outcome?

We can say it limits how often this proposed post-update barrier and copy-on-write capture are invoked: once per 1,000 steps. Whether that frequency keeps checkpoint-induced throughput loss within 5% is still the hypothesis. The interval alone does not establish the size of the cost when capture occurs or the resulting average throughput.
So the claim is not that step IDs guarantee identical model, optimizer, and RNG values?

Right. The claim is that this capture arrangement preserves identical *state step IDs* across ranks. For the larger checkpointing goal, the model, optimizer, and logical RNG snapshots must also form a coherent state for that step. Identical IDs describe alignment of the step designation, not equality of every distributed state value.
How should we state it in one sentence while keeping its uncertainty visible?

We hypothesize that, at 1,000-step intervals, a post-update rank barrier followed by copy-on-write capture will preserve identical state step IDs across ranks while limiting checkpoint-induced throughput loss to ≤5% relative to checkpoint-free training.

To evaluate the step-boundary capture hypothesis, let’s benchmark 8-rank training for 20,000 steps, checkpointing every 1,000 steps. We’ll compare state step IDs and tokens per second against checkpoint-free training.

That gives the proposed comparison a clear scope: 8 ranks, 20,000 training steps, and a checkpoint interval of 1,000 steps. The state step IDs address the alignment prediction for the post-update barrier and copy-on-write capture; tokens per second addresses the predicted throughput cost. Checkpoint-free training is the throughput baseline. This describes a benchmark to carry out, not results from one.
What should the state step ID comparison tell us?

It should tell us whether the checkpointed state carries the same logical step ID across the 8 ranks at each capture point. That directly examines the hypothesis’s prediction of identical state step IDs. It is distinct from measuring throughput: a run could exhibit matching IDs without meeting the performance bound, or meet the performance bound without matching IDs.
Should we compare IDs only at the end of the 20,000 steps?

The relevant points are the checkpoint captures made at the 1,000-step interval throughout the 20,000-step run. Looking only at the final state would not examine alignment at the earlier captures. The activity does not specify a particular log format or collection mechanism; it specifies comparing state step IDs as part of the benchmark.
Are the 1,000-step intervals themselves the variable we’re testing?

In this activity, 1,000 steps is the stated checkpoint interval, not a range of intervals to compare. The benchmark evaluates the capture hypothesis at that cadence during 8-rank training over 20,000 steps. It does not, as written, compare different checkpoint frequencies.
How does tokens per second connect to the ≤5% throughput-loss claim?

Tokens per second is the throughput measure for the comparison. To evaluate a loss of no more than 5% versus checkpoint-free training, compare the checkpointed run’s tokens per second with the checkpoint-free baseline’s tokens per second on a like-for-like basis. The bound corresponds to checkpointed throughput being at least 95% of the checkpoint-free throughput. No measured tokens-per-second values are given here.
Could I instead report how many seconds a checkpoint upload takes?

That might describe one part of checkpointing, but it would not replace the specified throughput comparison. The hypothesis concerns the effect on training throughput, and this activity calls for tokens per second against checkpoint-free training. Capture, coordination, and asynchronous work can all affect that overall measure; upload duration alone would not establish a ≤5% throughput loss.
What does the checkpoint-free run contribute to the step ID comparison?

Its stated role is the throughput baseline. The state step ID comparison concerns whether the checkpoint captures agree across ranks. Checkpoint-free training does not provide checkpoint captures to compare in the same way. The activity calls for both comparisons, but they answer different parts of the hypothesis.
Is it important that the baseline also be an 8-rank training comparison over 20,000 steps?

For a meaningful throughput comparison, the checkpoint-free baseline should be like-for-like with the stated 8-rank, 20,000-step benchmark except for checkpointing. Otherwise a difference in tokens per second could reflect differences other than checkpointing. The activity identifies the training scale and duration; it does not supply measured baseline performance.
Do matching IDs prove that optimizer and RNG contents are consistent?

Not by themselves. Matching state step IDs would address the specific prediction about step designations across ranks. It would not independently prove that the model, optimizer, and logical RNG contents actually correspond to those IDs. The benchmark, as stated, compares IDs and tokens per second; we should not describe it as a full validation of checkpoint contents.
Then why measure step IDs at all?

Because identical IDs across ranks are an explicit prediction of the hypothesis being evaluated. The comparison can reveal whether that proposed alignment property appears at the scheduled captures. It is useful evidence about that property, even though the larger requirement of a committed, globally consistent recoverable state calls for more than an ID comparison.
Could the tokens-per-second comparison alone tell us whether the barrier aligned the ranks?

No. Tokens per second measures training throughput, not agreement on the captured logical step. That is why the activity includes state step IDs as a separate comparison. Neither measurement should be used as a substitute for the other.

Rejection needs to be based on the shard’s actual relationship to the selected logical step, rather than making an inconsistent candidate appear consistent in its metadata. The proposal does not specify how that relationship is verified beyond the step-ID question.
Does rejecting a mixed-step shard mean training has to stop and retake the checkpoint immediately?

No immediate stop or retake is specified. Rejection before manifest commit means that an inconsistent candidate must not become a committed checkpoint. Training progress and checkpoint eligibility are distinct. Whether the checkpointing system attempts another candidate, and when, is not decided by this question.
Then what does “without stalling training” require us to be careful about?

The consistency decision should not require ranks to wait at a new checkpoint barrier while uploads are checked. But avoiding an explicit barrier does not automatically avoid throughput effects: capture, staging, uploads, and checks can still compete with training. The intended behavior is to let training proceed while the candidate remains uncommitted, subject to the broader limit of no more than 5% checkpoint-induced throughput loss versus checkpoint-free training.
Is withholding manifest commit itself a training stall?

Not necessarily. It is a delay in declaring a checkpoint recoverable, which is different from pausing training. The distinction holds only if the implementation can keep doing checkpoint work without forcing training to wait for that decision. The question asks how to achieve that; it does not establish that every way of withholding commit will be stall-free.
Where does the atomic manifest help in this situation?

It gives a clear point at which a complete candidate becomes a committed checkpoint. Before that point, uploaded shards can be examined without exposing a mixed-step collection as recoverable. The atomic commit should occur only for a candidate that passes the required checks. Atomicity protects the visibility of the decision; it cannot correct a mixture that the checks fail to detect.
Could an upload stall cause a manifest to commit with only the shards that arrived on time?

That would not satisfy the proposed ordering if a delayed shard is required: globally indexed shards are uploaded before the atomic manifest commit. A stall can leave a candidate pending, but it does not justify declaring an incomplete training state committed. This says what a valid commit must avoid, not how long the pending state can be maintained without affecting training.
Are globally indexed shards relevant to rejecting a mixed-step candidate?

They help identify what portion of the overall checkpoint each shard is supposed to represent, independently of its original worker placement. That makes it possible to reason about which portions are present and which belong together, including when a restore uses another tensor-parallel layout. Global indexing alone does not establish step alignment; the candidate still needs a consistent model, optimizer, and logical RNG state.
What if each rank has a matching step ID, but the optimizer portion on one rank was actually captured earlier?

Then the IDs would be misleading and an ID-only gate would not be sufficient. The requirement is for the captured optimizer portion to correspond to the same logical training state as the other portions, not just to carry the same identifier. This is a limit on what a simple comparison can establish; the question does not provide a content-validation mechanism.
Does post-sync capture remove the need for that concern?

No. Post-sync capture is the proposed capture point for the barrier-free approach, but the concern is whether the resulting model, optimizer, and logical RNG contents actually correspond across ranks. The manifest decision cannot assume that post-sync capture was successful solely because it was intended to be post-sync.
Could the checker accept model shards first and decide about optimizer and RNG later?

It could evaluate available pieces incrementally, but it must not *commit the checkpoint* on the strength of model shards alone. The final recoverable unit has to include a globally consistent model, optimizer, and RNG state. An early provisional observation about one component is not the same as approval of the whole candidate.
Do rejected shards have to be deleted before training can proceed?

The question does not specify deletion or retention behavior. What matters for consistency is that mixed-step shards are not used to justify an atomic manifest commit for an inconsistent candidate. Storage cleanup is a separate implementation concern, and we cannot assume either that it blocks training or that it is free.
Could we say that the commit check happens off the training path?

You can state that as an aim for barrier-free checking, provided it is not presented as an established implementation property. More precisely: let training continue while staged uploads are checked, and keep any candidate that fails or has not completed those checks uncommitted. Whether doing so avoids stalls and keeps throughput loss within 5% still needs to be established.
If uploads fall behind, can we promise that training will never feel backpressure?

No such promise follows from staging or from withholding commit. An implementation may face limits on resources used by pending checkpoint work; the supplied question does not say how those limits are handled. The honest distinction is that rejection need not be implemented as an explicit training barrier, but its actual throughput impact is not known here.
How would a single-worker crash interact with an uncommitted candidate containing mixed-step shards?

That candidate should not be treated as a recoverable checkpoint, whether or not a worker crashes. The recovery requirement is to use a *committed*, globally consistent model, optimizer, and RNG state after any single-worker crash. The barrier-free checking question concerns preventing an invalid candidate from crossing the commit boundary; it does not itself demonstrate crash recovery.
So the key distinction is between rejecting a checkpoint candidate and interrupting training?

Yes. Rejecting mixed-step shards from a candidate means refusing to commit that candidate as a complete checkpoint. It need not mean stopping training to resolve the candidate immediately. The open engineering question is whether this separation can be maintained under upload delays without creating a training stall or exceeding the throughput-loss target.
What is the most careful answer to the original question?

Have barrier-free uploads remain provisional until the required globally indexed model, optimizer, and logical RNG shards are present and verified as belonging to one logical step; commit their manifest atomically only then. If a required shard conflicts, do not commit that mixed-step candidate. Let training continue while upload and checking proceed rather than making ranks wait for the commit decision—but treat the absence of stalls and compliance with the 5% throughput-loss limit as properties to establish, not guaranteed consequences of this description.

Here’s a hypothesis for the barrier-free upload question: a coordinator commits only complete, matching step-tagged shard sets. That should prevent mixed snapshots without exceeding 5% throughput loss under upload stalls.

That is a proposed commit rule with two predictions, not a demonstrated outcome. The consistency prediction is that an incomplete set, or one containing shards tagged for different steps, cannot become a committed snapshot. The performance prediction is that applying this rule under upload stalls keeps checkpoint-induced throughput loss at no more than 5% versus checkpoint-free training.
What is the coordinator deciding, exactly?

It decides whether a candidate set of uploaded shards is eligible to be committed as one checkpoint. Under the hypothesis, eligibility requires both completeness and matching step tags. The coordinator is not being assumed to repair mismatched shards; it withholds commitment unless the candidate meets those conditions.
Why specify both complete and matching? Wouldn’t matching tags be enough?

No. Tags can match among the shards that have arrived while a required shard is still missing. That would leave an incomplete candidate, even though no mismatch is visible among its available pieces. Conversely, having every required shard does not help if some belong to different steps. The hypothesis makes both properties prerequisites for commit.
What counts as a complete set in this context?

Conceptually, it is the set of shards required to represent the checkpointed training state, including its model, optimizer, and logical RNG portions. Global indexing from the proposed design provides a way to identify what portions a candidate is supposed to contain. The hypothesis does not specify a shard count, a manifest schema, or a particular method for deciding that every required portion is present.
Does matching mean all ranks have identical shard contents?

No. It means the step tags for the shards in a candidate agree on the logical training step. Different ranks may contribute different portions of the state. Neither matching tags nor the word “complete” implies that every rank stores numerically identical model, optimizer, or RNG values.
Then is it accurate to say this prevents every possible inconsistency?

That would overstate the hypothesis. The proposed rule is directed at preventing *mixed snapshots* from being committed by excluding incomplete or differently step-tagged shard sets. Matching tags alone cannot prove that a shard’s contents actually correspond to its tag, or establish every property needed for recovery. The hypothesis predicts that the commit rule prevents mixed snapshots; it has not established that prediction.
Could a shard with the wrong step tag simply be relabeled to complete the set?

Relabeling would not change the captured state inside the shard. Under the proposed rule, a shard whose tag does not match the candidate step makes that candidate ineligible for commit as assembled. The hypothesis does not prescribe whether that shard is retained, discarded, or considered for some other candidate.
What happens to a candidate when an upload stalls?

If the stall leaves a required shard unavailable, the candidate is not yet complete and therefore is not eligible for commit. The coordinator’s rule can defer the commit decision without treating the partial upload as a recoverable checkpoint. Whether that deferral affects training throughput is the separate performance prediction in the hypothesis.
Could the coordinator commit the shards that arrived and add the delayed one later?

Not as one complete checkpoint under this rule. Commitment is reserved for a complete, matching step-tagged shard set. Presenting an incomplete candidate as committed and filling it in later would erase the distinction the hypothesis relies on between work in progress and a recoverable checkpoint.
Is the commit meant to be the atomic manifest commit from the checkpoint proposal?

It can be understood as the eligibility decision preceding that proposed atomic manifest commit. The coordinator would permit commitment only for a complete, matching set; the atomic manifest commit would then mark the checkpoint as committed. The hypothesis does not specify the coordinator’s internal protocol or a new manifest implementation.
Does introducing a coordinator necessarily mean training waits for it?

Not necessarily. Checkpoint commitment and training progress are conceptually separate: a candidate can remain uncommitted while uploads and checks proceed. But a coordinator is not automatically free of coordination costs or backpressure. The hypothesis specifically predicts that its rule can operate under upload stalls without pushing checkpoint-induced throughput loss above 5%; that remains to be established.
So “without exceeding 5%” is about the whole training run, not just coordinator processing time?

Yes. The comparison is training throughput with checkpointing versus checkpoint-free training. The ≤5% target covers checkpoint-induced effects as a whole, including any effects associated with staging, uploads, and the commit decision. A quick coordinator decision alone would not demonstrate that the overall throughput bound holds under upload stalls.
Could preventing mixed commits actually make checkpoints less frequent when uploads stall?

A stalled required upload can leave a candidate pending rather than committed, so the rule does not promise a particular commit frequency. The hypothesis is about preventing mixed snapshots and maintaining the throughput bound under upload stalls. It does not state how many candidates would commit, how long one may remain pending, or what checkpoint interval would result.
Does a pending checkpoint count as the committed state we need after a single-worker crash?

No. A pending candidate is not a committed checkpoint. The broader recovery requirement calls for a committed, globally consistent model, optimizer, and RNG state after any single-worker crash. This hypothesis addresses the gate that should keep incomplete or mixed-step candidates from being committed; it does not by itself demonstrate crash recovery.
How does the coordinator know which shards belong together without tying restore to the original workers?

The proposed globally indexed shards provide the relevant conceptual basis: shard identity describes a portion of the overall checkpoint, rather than only which worker uploaded it. The coordinator could use those identities and step tags to reason about a candidate set. The hypothesis does not specify the indexing format, and its commit rule alone does not establish a successful restore across tensor-parallel layouts.
Would one matching tag for the set be enough, or do model, optimizer, and RNG each matter?

They each matter to the recoverable state. The intended matching set must cover the required model, optimizer, and logical RNG shards for the same logical step; a model-only collection with matching tags would not be a complete training-state checkpoint. The hypothesis does not define how tags are stored, but the consistency condition cannot ignore either optimizer or RNG state.
Suppose every required shard is present and every tag matches. Can we then say a restore under a new tensor-parallel layout works?

Not on that basis alone. Completeness and matching step tags govern whether the candidate may be committed under this hypothesis. Cross-layout restore also requires the committed state to be reconstructible under a different tensor-parallel layout. The globally indexed shard proposal is relevant to that aim, but this commit-rule hypothesis does not report a restore.
What observation would address the mixed-snapshot prediction most directly?

The direct question is whether a candidate with missing required shards or conflicting step tags is withheld from commit, while any committed candidate is a complete set with matching step tags. That examines the coordinator rule as stated. It would still be important not to equate tag agreement alone with proof of the underlying state contents or of successful recovery.
And what observation addresses the performance prediction?

Compare training throughput with this checkpointing approach under upload stalls against checkpoint-free training, then determine whether the checkpoint-induced loss is at most 5%. No throughput measurement for this coordinator hypothesis is supplied, so the performance prediction cannot yet be stated as a result.
If it prevents mixed commits but throughput loss exceeds 5%, how should we characterize the hypothesis?

The consistency prediction would have an observation in its favor, but the combined hypothesis would not meet its performance prediction under those conditions. The reverse distinction also matters: throughput within 5% would not compensate for committing a mixed or incomplete shard set. Both outcomes have to be assessed without substituting one for the other.
Can you restate the hypothesis in a way that keeps the upload-stall condition and the uncertainty explicit?

We hypothesize that, under upload stalls, a coordinator that commits only complete sets of shards with matching step tags will prevent mixed snapshots while keeping checkpoint-induced throughput loss at or below 5% versus checkpoint-free training. It is a proposed commit rule and performance prediction, not yet a measured result.

Do the model, optimizer, and RNG portions all matter to that complete set?

What should throughput be compared with?

The performance target in the coordinator hypothesis is checkpoint-induced throughput loss of no more than 5% versus checkpoint-free training. Is the 5% figure a limit on coordinator validation time for each snapshot?

Does “20,000 stalled steps” mean every individual training step must pause for an upload?

No. It describes a 20,000-step benchmark under upload stalls, not a requirement to stop training on every step. The activity does not state the stall schedule or say that each step is stalled. We should preserve the benchmark condition without adding a particular pattern of delays.
Should we assume those stalls last the same amount of time as in the earlier stress activity?

This activity says to benchmark 20,000 stalled steps but does not specify a stall duration. We should not insert a duration into this benchmark description or claim that a particular schedule was used. The stated condition is upload stalls; the stated observations are mixed commits and throughput.
Does the activity include a worker crash during those 20,000 steps?

No worker crash is specified. The benchmark examines coordinator behavior and throughput under upload stalls. It does not, as stated, demonstrate recovery of a committed checkpoint after any single-worker crash.
Or a restore under a different tensor-parallel layout?

No cross-layout restore is specified either. Coordinator validation concerns which shard sets may be committed, and this benchmark concerns mixed commits and throughput. Suppose the replay rejects the mixed candidates but the benchmark records a mixed commit. How would we describe that?

What if there are no mixed commits, but throughput loss exceeds 5%?

Replay the four mixed-step snapshots through coordinator validation, then benchmark 20,000 training steps under upload stalls, checking for mixed commits and measuring throughput against checkpoint-free training to assess the ≤5% loss prediction.

Does a committed snapshot with matching step IDs establish that its model, optimizer, and RNG contents are recoverable?

Was a single-worker crash injected during this benchmark?

No cross-layout restore is reported. The result concerns coordinator validation and stalled training; it does not show a committed snapshot being restored under a different tensor-parallel layout.

How can I report this without implying we know what happened to the other four benchmark snapshots?

For the restore side, I propose loading committed manifests, resharding globally indexed model and optimizer tensors across tensor-parallel degrees, and remapping logical RNG streams.

That gives the restore path three distinct responsibilities. It starts from a committed manifest rather than an unfinished checkpoint candidate. It then uses the global indexing of model and optimizer tensors to reconstruct their portions for the tensor-parallel degree used at restore. Finally, it remaps the logical RNG streams so RNG state remains part of the restored training state. This is a proposal for supporting cross-layout restores, not a report that a restore has succeeded.
Why start with a committed manifest instead of any shards that are already available?

Available shards may still belong to checkpoint work in progress. A committed manifest identifies a checkpoint eligible to be treated as a complete recoverable unit. Starting there preserves the distinction between a state selected for recovery and a collection of uploaded pieces that has not been committed. The proposal does not specify how manifests are stored or discovered.
Does the manifest itself contain the model, optimizer, and RNG state?

The proposal does not prescribe what the manifest contains. Its role here is to identify the committed checkpoint to restore. The model and optimizer tensors are described as globally indexed and subject to resharding, while logical RNG streams are subject to remapping. We should not infer a particular division of bytes between the manifest and its associated checkpoint data.
What does “globally indexed” buy us during restore?

It makes a saved tensor portion identifiable by its place in the overall model or optimizer state, rather than only by the worker or tensor-parallel partition that held it during checkpointing. That gives the restore process a basis for assigning the saved portions to a different tensor-parallel layout. The proposal does not specify the index format or the mechanics of moving those portions.
Could we simply send each saved worker’s data to the worker with the same number?

That would make the restore depend on the original worker assignment, which is not sufficient as a general description of restoring across tensor-parallel degrees. The proposal instead calls for resharding globally indexed tensors according to the restore layout. It does not prohibit a particular transfer when it happens to be appropriate; it says the interpretation of the saved state cannot rely solely on matching worker numbers.
Are we changing the mathematical model when we reshard it?

Resharding, as proposed here, changes how the saved model state is distributed for the target tensor-parallel degree. It is not a proposal to train a different model or alter the saved values merely to fit the layout. The requirement is to recover a globally consistent training state even though its physical partitioning may differ.
Why explicitly include optimizer tensors in the resharding step?

Because a cross-layout restore of model tensors alone would not restore the complete training state. Optimizer state has to remain associated with the corresponding recovered model state, and its saved tensor portions may also need to be distributed according to the target tensor-parallel degree. The proposal names both model and optimizer tensors to avoid treating optimizer recovery as an afterthought.
Does “across tensor-parallel degrees” mean only one particular change in degree?

No particular source or target degree is named. The proposal is to support resharding between tensor-parallel layouts, including a restore whose degree differs from the checkpoint’s layout. It does not specify a list of supported degrees or claim that every conceivable layout has been tested.
What is the logical RNG stream doing alongside the tensors?

RNG state is part of the training state that must be recovered. Describing it as logical streams lets the restore proposal address RNG identity separately from the rank or partition that happened to hold an RNG state at checkpoint time. Remapping those streams is intended to carry the checkpoint’s RNG state into the restore layout rather than simply dropping it or assigning it by an assumed one-to-one worker match.
Does remapping logical RNG streams promise identical future random draws under every layout?

That promise is not stated. The proposal requires a remapping of the logical RNG streams as part of restoring the checkpointed state. It does not define the mapping or assert that all future draws, in every ordering under every tensor-parallel degree, will be identical. Those would be more specific claims than this proposal makes.
So we need to keep logical RNG separate from the physical rank number?

That is the conceptual point of calling the streams logical and remapping them. If RNG state were interpreted only as a particular rank’s local artifact, a changed tensor-parallel layout could make its assignment ambiguous. The proposal calls for an interpretation that remains meaningful across layouts, without specifying the representation or remapping rule.
Would loading a committed manifest alone establish global consistency?

Not by itself. Commitment identifies the checkpoint selected for recovery; the restore must also reconstruct the corresponding model, optimizer, and logical RNG state coherently. A manifest cannot compensate for incorrectly resharded tensors or an incompatible RNG remapping. The proposal combines these actions because recovery concerns the training state as a whole.
Could the model and optimizer each be resharded independently, as long as they both load?

They have to remain consistent parts of the same committed training state. The proposal does not require identical physical partitioning for their tensors, but merely loading each component is not enough if the reconstructed optimizer state no longer corresponds to the reconstructed model state. The restore should preserve their relationship while distributing both for the target tensor-parallel degree.
What happens if some needed portion of a committed checkpoint cannot be read?

The proposed restore cannot be considered a successful recovery of the full training state if a required model, optimizer, or RNG portion is unavailable. Starting from a committed manifest expresses which checkpoint is eligible for recovery, but this proposal does not specify storage-failure handling or a fallback procedure. We should not assume either outcome.
Does this restore proposal also cover a crash of any one worker?

It is meant to serve the broader requirement: after any single-worker crash, recovery must use a committed, globally consistent model, optimizer, and RNG state. Starting from committed manifests and reconstructing all three components is relevant to that requirement. The proposal itself does not report a crash injection or establish that recovery succeeds for every possible single-worker crash.
Is a layout change required whenever recovery follows a crash?

No. The design must support recovery after a single-worker crash and restores across tensor-parallel layouts, but it does not say every crash changes the tensor-parallel degree. This restore proposal accommodates a target layout that may differ from the saved one; it does not make such a change mandatory for each recovery.
Where does the checkpoint throughput target fit into this restore description?

The overall design must limit checkpoint-induced training-throughput loss to 5% versus checkpoint-free training. This proposal describes how to restore a committed checkpoint, rather than reporting training-throughput measurements. Its cross-layout reconstruction steps should not be mistaken for evidence that the checkpointing system meets the 5% target.
Could I claim that global indexing makes cross-layout restoration automatic?

No. Global indexing supplies a way to interpret which portions of model and optimizer state were saved. The restore still has to reshard those tensors for the target tensor-parallel degree and remap logical RNG streams. The proposal identifies those responsibilities; it does not claim they have been implemented or verified.
What is a concise description that retains all three pieces of the restore plan?

How should globally indexed Adam moments and logical RNG streams map from TP=8 to TP=4 without changing resumed updates?

The mapping should be defined by the logical training state, not by the ranks that held it under TP=8. What does global indexing need to identify for an Adam moment?

It needs to identify which portion of which optimizer-state tensor the moment represents, so that portion remains paired with the corresponding model parameter portion after resharding. Would each TP=4 rank just take the data from two TP=8 ranks?

Not as a general rule. Halving the tensor-parallel degree does not, by itself, establish that each new rank should receive exactly two old ranks’ artifacts.
