For failure recovery, I propose persisting checksum-verified shards in durable object storage, fencing stale worker epochs, and restoring only complete, atomically committed manifests.

That proposal separates three safeguards. Checksum verification addresses the integrity of persisted shards; durable object storage is where they remain available for recovery. Epoch fencing prevents a stale worker from participating as though it belonged to the current worker generation. Requiring a complete, atomically committed manifest keeps a partial checkpoint from being selected for restore. These are proposed design rules, not a report that crash recovery has been demonstrated.
What does “checksum-verified” mean in this proposal?

It means shard integrity is checked using a checksum rather than assuming that persisted bytes are valid merely because an upload completed. The proposal does not specify a checksum algorithm, when every check occurs, or the format in which checksums are recorded. The relevant recovery property is that shards used for a committed restore have passed the required integrity check.
Does a valid checksum tell us that a shard belongs to the right training step?

No. A checksum can check integrity of the bytes against an expected value; it does not establish that the shard belongs to the same logical training step as the rest of a checkpoint. Step consistency and shard integrity are distinct. A complete, committed manifest must identify a coherent checkpoint, while checksum verification addresses the integrity of its persisted pieces.
Why specify durable object storage rather than just saying the shards were uploaded?

An upload event alone is not the same as having shards available from a durable location when recovery is needed. The proposal explicitly places checksum-verified shards in durable object storage as part of the recoverable checkpoint. It does not specify a storage provider, durability level, replication scheme, or availability guarantee beyond that description.
Is this saying each worker keeps its own shard available after it crashes?

No. Persisting shards in durable object storage is meant to avoid treating a worker’s local availability as the sole source for recovery. The proposal does not require a crashed worker to come back and serve its shards. It also does not, by itself, prove recovery after any single-worker crash; that remains a property to establish.
What does fencing a stale worker epoch do?

It draws a boundary between the current worker epoch and an older one. A worker acting under a stale epoch should not be able to affect checkpoint state or the restore decision as though it were current. The proposal calls for that exclusion but does not specify how epochs are assigned, how fencing is enforced, or what happens to the worker afterward.
Is an epoch the same as a training step?

No. A training-step identifier associates model, optimizer, and RNG state with a logical point in training. A worker epoch distinguishes whether worker activity belongs to the current worker generation or is stale. Agreement on step IDs would not, on its own, fence an old worker epoch, and a current epoch would not by itself prove step alignment.
Suppose an old worker finishes an upload late. Does fencing mean its bytes must be deleted?

Deletion is not specified. The important proposed rule is that stale-epoch activity cannot be treated as authorized to affect a committed checkpoint or current restore. How an implementation handles bytes left by stale activity is a separate storage-management question. We should not equate fencing with a particular cleanup procedure.
Could we say the old worker’s late shard may be used if its checksum matches?

A matching checksum alone would not settle that. Integrity does not establish that stale-epoch activity is eligible to contribute to the checkpoint selected for recovery. The proposal includes fencing precisely to keep stale workers from crossing that boundary, alongside checks on shard integrity and manifest completeness.
What is meant by a complete manifest here?

It means the manifest selected for restore describes a complete checkpoint, rather than a partial set of persisted shards. For the recovery goal, that checkpoint has to encompass the required model, optimizer, and RNG state. The proposal does not prescribe the manifest fields, shard count, or method of establishing completeness.
Does a complete manifest mean every possible shard ever uploaded has to be in it?

No. Completeness concerns the shards required for the particular checkpoint the manifest commits, not every shard produced by checkpoint work. Uploads that are provisional or belong to a different candidate are not automatically part of that checkpoint. The proposal does not specify how such uploads are managed.
Why insist that manifest commitment be atomic?

Atomic commitment gives recovery a clear all-or-nothing decision about whether the complete manifest is committed. Without that boundary, a restore might mistake a partially published checkpoint for a recoverable one. The proposal does not name an atomic-commit mechanism; it states the property required before a manifest can be used for restore.
If half the shards are durable, could we atomically commit a manifest listing just that half?

Not as a complete checkpoint if the other half is required. Atomic commitment governs how the decision becomes visible; it does not turn an incomplete collection into a complete model, optimizer, and RNG state. This proposal permits restores only from manifests that are both complete and atomically committed.
Does atomic commitment by itself prove that the referenced shards pass checksum verification?

No. These are separate conditions in the proposal. A committed manifest identifies the checkpoint eligible for restore; checksum verification concerns the integrity of the persisted shards used by that checkpoint. Neither condition replaces the other, and atomicity cannot correct a corrupted or unavailable required shard.
What if a required shard fails its checksum check during restore?

That shard should not be treated as verified, so the proposed restore cannot claim to have reconstructed the complete training state from that checkpoint on the strength of the manifest alone. The proposal does not specify a repair, retry, or fallback procedure. It only states that the shards are checksum-verified and that restores use complete, atomically committed manifests.
Should we interpret “restore only complete, atomically committed manifests” as restoring the manifest instead of the training state?

No. The manifest identifies the eligible checkpoint; restoring means reconstructing its model, optimizer, and RNG state from the required persisted shards. The phrase restricts which manifest can authorize that reconstruction. Loading a manifest without recovering its corresponding training state would not meet the recovery goal.
Could there be several uploaded shard sets but only one eligible for restore?

Conceptually, yes: uploaded or provisional checkpoint work need not all be eligible for recovery. The proposal’s eligibility test is a complete, atomically committed manifest with the necessary checksum-verified shards, subject to stale-epoch fencing. It does not say how many candidates or committed checkpoints are retained.
How do these rules help with a crash of any single worker?

The intended recovery path does not depend on reading state from the crashed worker: it selects a complete committed manifest and uses its checksum-verified shards in durable object storage. Fencing is intended to prevent stale worker activity from interfering with that state or its restoration. Those rules address the failure-recovery requirement, but the proposal alone is not an observed test of every possible single-worker crash.
Does fencing imply that the crash itself automatically commits an in-progress checkpoint?

No. A worker failure cannot turn an incomplete or uncommitted candidate into a committed one. Fencing concerns stale worker epochs, while atomic manifest commitment determines which complete checkpoint is eligible for restore. After a crash, the proposed rule still restricts recovery to an already complete, atomically committed manifest.
What if the manifest is committed but some shard is still being uploaded?

If that shard is required for the manifest’s checkpoint, calling the manifest complete would be inconsistent with the proposed rule. The restore restriction is meant to keep a checkpoint from becoming eligible before its required shards are persisted and verifiable. The proposal does not spell out the upload-to-commit coordination mechanism.
Do these safeguards guarantee the optimizer and RNG state correspond to the model?

Not by themselves. Shard checksums, durable storage, epoch fencing, and atomic commitment protect integrity, availability, and the eligibility boundary. The contents of the checkpoint must still represent a globally consistent model, optimizer, and RNG state. A complete manifest cannot make mismatched training-state versions consistent merely by committing them.
Does durable storage decide how the checkpoint is restored under a different tensor-parallel layout?

No. Durable storage keeps the saved shards available; it does not decide how globally indexed model and optimizer tensors are resharded or logical RNG streams remapped. The cross-layout restore proposal addresses that interpretation. This failure-recovery proposal adds safeguards around which persisted checkpoint can be trusted as a source.
Could a checksum be valid after resharding even if the state was put in the wrong place?

A checksum of saved shard bytes would not, by itself, validate the placement of those bytes in a new tensor-parallel layout. Integrity of the persisted shard and correctness of cross-layout reconstruction are different properties. Both matter if the restored model, optimizer, and RNG state is to be globally consistent.
Do we know whether these checks will stay within the 5% checkpoint-throughput-loss limit?

No throughput result is supplied for this proposal. Persisting and verifying shards, fencing epochs, and committing manifests can have costs, so they must fit the broader limit of no more than 5% checkpoint-induced throughput loss versus checkpoint-free training. The proposal does not quantify those costs or claim that the limit has been measured.
Can we characterize this as eliminating all possible storage failures?

No. Durable object storage and checksum verification are proposed safeguards, not a claim that storage can never fail or that every damaged shard can be recovered. The stated design objective remains recovery of a committed, globally consistent state after any single-worker crash; broader failure modes and repair guarantees are not specified here.
How would you state the proposed recovery rule compactly?

Persist checksum-verified checkpoint shards in durable object storage, fence stale worker epochs, and restore model, optimizer, and RNG state only from complete, atomically committed manifests. This defines the proposed eligibility and integrity boundary without claiming a completed crash-recovery test or a measured throughput result.
If a worker crashes during upload, can epoch fencing prevent its delayed shards from entering a replacement worker’s committed manifest?

Yes, if fencing governs which shard contributions are eligible for that manifest—not merely which workers are allowed to start new uploads. A delayed shard associated with a stale worker epoch may still arrive in durable object storage, but arrival should not authorize its inclusion in a replacement worker’s checkpoint. Before atomic commit, the candidate manifest would need to exclude stale-epoch contributions and contain a complete, consistent set of eligible shards. Whether a particular implementation enforces that boundary remains to be established.
So fencing does not necessarily stop the delayed upload itself?

Correct. Preventing bytes from arriving and preventing those bytes from entering a committed manifest are different properties. For this question, the decisive property is that a late shard from the stale epoch cannot become part of the replacement worker’s committed checkpoint simply because its upload finishes.
What makes the shard stale: the time it arrives or the worker epoch it belongs to?

The relevant distinction is the worker epoch under which the shard was contributed, not just its arrival time. An upload can be delayed, so arrival order alone cannot establish whether it belongs to the replacement worker’s candidate checkpoint. The proposal does not specify how that epoch association is represented or checked.
Does the crash automatically make every shard the worker ever uploaded unusable?

No such blanket rule follows. The question concerns delayed shards from the crashed worker entering a replacement worker’s *newly committed manifest*. It should not be confused with changing the status of an already complete, atomically committed checkpoint. Fencing stale activity protects the new commit boundary; it does not, by itself, erase previously committed state.
Suppose the delayed shard has exactly the model values the replacement needs. Could the manifest include it on that basis?

Matching apparent values would not, by itself, authorize a stale-epoch contribution to the replacement worker’s manifest. Epoch eligibility is a separate condition from whether bytes look useful. The candidate also needs the required model, optimizer, and RNG portions to represent one globally consistent state. The question does not provide a rule for adopting an old shard as a new worker’s contribution.
What if its checksum passes?

A passing checksum addresses shard integrity, not epoch eligibility. A shard can be intact and still be an ineligible stale contribution to the manifest being assembled. Conversely, an eligible contribution would still need to meet the integrity and consistency requirements. Neither check replaces the other.
Could matching step IDs make the old epoch acceptable?

Not automatically. A matching step ID addresses the logical training step the shard purports to represent; an epoch addresses whether the worker’s contribution is authorized for the candidate being committed. The replacement worker’s manifest must not admit a delayed stale-epoch shard merely because its step ID matches other shards. Matching labels also do not independently prove that their contents are consistent.
Where does the fence have to matter if the upload was already in progress when the crash occurred?

It has to matter at least when the system decides which shards may be referenced by the replacement worker’s manifest. Otherwise an in-flight upload could finish after the worker is stale and still be incorporated at commit time. The question does not prescribe a particular fencing mechanism; it identifies the eligibility decision that the fence must protect.
Would checking eligibility only when an upload begins be sufficient?

Not for the delayed-upload case on its own. An upload might begin while its worker epoch is current but finish after a crash and replacement. If the manifest then accepts the shard solely because it passed an earlier check, that earlier check would not enforce the intended boundary at commitment. The candidate’s eligibility needs to hold when it is committed.
Does the replacement worker’s arrival instantly make a partially assembled checkpoint complete?

No. Replacing a worker does not supply any missing model, optimizer, or RNG portions or make mixed contributions consistent. The manifest must still describe a complete eligible shard set before it can be atomically committed. An unfinished upload remains unfinished checkpoint work regardless of the worker change.
Could a manifest list the delayed shard provisionally and remove it before commit?

The important rule is about what becomes *committed*. Provisional checkpoint work can be distinguished from the complete manifest eligible for atomic commit. A delayed stale-epoch shard must not remain in the replacement worker’s committed manifest. The proposal does not prescribe whether provisional descriptions are maintained or edited along the way.
If the late shard is rejected, does training have to wait for it to be deleted?

Deletion is not a stated prerequisite for training to proceed or for a different complete checkpoint to be considered. Fencing concerns whether stale activity may affect commitment; it does not specify cleanup of bytes already stored. That distinction also avoids assuming that storage cleanup is instantaneous or cost-free.
Can the replacement commit the other shards and simply omit the stale one?

Only if the resulting set is complete for that checkpoint. If the omitted shard represents a required portion of the model, optimizer, or RNG state and there is no eligible corresponding portion, committing the remainder would create an incomplete checkpoint. Fencing cannot justify weakening the completeness requirement.
Would atomic manifest commit alone stop the stale shard from entering?

No. Atomicity makes the commit decision all-or-nothing, but it does not decide whether the proposed members are eligible. An atomic manifest could still reference the wrong shards if eligibility is not checked. Epoch fencing must apply to that membership decision, while completeness, step consistency, and checksum verification address other requirements.
Is it enough to fence the crashed worker from writing a manifest?

Not necessarily. The replacement worker might assemble a manifest using a shard whose upload was initiated by the old epoch. Preventing the stale worker from committing directly would not prevent that indirect inclusion. The question specifically asks whether stale shards can enter the replacement worker’s committed manifest, so eligibility must cover referenced shards as well as who requests the commit.
Could two shards with the same global index but different epochs both appear in that manifest?

A complete, globally interpretable checkpoint should not treat two conflicting contributions for the same required portion as though both were the one intended state. The epoch distinction would help identify which contribution is stale, but this question does not specify a rule for resolving every duplicate or conflict. What it does require is that a stale-epoch shard not slip into the replacement worker’s committed set.
How does global indexing help, and what does it not solve?

Global indexing identifies which portion of the overall checkpoint a shard represents, independently of its original worker placement. That helps determine whether the candidate has the required portions. It does not identify, by itself, whether the contributor’s worker epoch is eligible, whether the bytes pass checksum verification, or whether model, optimizer, and RNG portions belong to one logical step.
If the replacement is preparing a checkpoint for the same training step, is the epoch distinction still relevant?

Yes. Step identity and worker-epoch eligibility answer different questions. Even if two contributions claim the same training step, the replacement worker’s candidate should not silently accept a contribution fenced as stale. The manifest needs an eligible, complete, globally consistent shard set; agreement on a step designation alone cannot establish all three properties.
What should recovery do if the worker crashes before the replacement has a complete manifest?

It should not treat that incomplete candidate as a committed checkpoint. The recovery requirement is to use a complete, atomically committed manifest representing a globally consistent model, optimizer, and RNG state after any single-worker crash. This question does not say how far back the eligible committed checkpoint may be or prescribe how the replacement finishes later checkpoint work.
Could we say the fence protects checkpoint creation but has no role in restore?

That would be too strong. Its immediate role in this question is to keep stale contributions out of the manifest before commit. Restore then selects only a complete, atomically committed manifest and its verified shards. The proposal does not specify a separate restore-time epoch procedure, so we should not invent one—or assert that epoch eligibility could never matter to interpreting a manifest.
Does this also guarantee a restore across a changed tensor-parallel degree?

No. Fencing protects which contributions may enter a committed checkpoint; it does not reshard globally indexed model and optimizer tensors or remap logical RNG streams for another tensor-parallel layout. Those are separate restore responsibilities. A manifest can be protected from stale shards without that fact alone demonstrating cross-layout recovery.
What about the 5% checkpoint-induced throughput-loss limit?

The broader limit remains no more than 5% versus checkpoint-free training. Epoch checks and delayed-upload handling could affect checkpoint work or training throughput, but this question provides no measurement. We cannot infer that enforcing the fence meets—or exceeds—the performance bound merely from the proposed rule.
Can we formulate the answer without claiming a crash test has passed?

Yes: epoch fencing can prevent a crashed worker’s delayed shards from entering a replacement worker’s committed manifest if shard eligibility is checked against the current epoch when the complete candidate is committed. A late upload may still exist, but it must not become an authorized member of that manifest. This is the condition the design must enforce, not an observed crash-recovery result.

Here’s a hypothesis for the worker-replacement case: epoch-scoped shard keys plus compare-and-swap manifest commits will reject late uploads after replacement and preserve the previous recoverable checkpoint.

That proposes two linked safeguards. Epoch-scoped shard keys distinguish shards contributed under different worker epochs; compare-and-swap commits make a manifest update conditional rather than allowing an unconditional replacement. The prediction is that a late upload from the old epoch will not enter the replacement worker’s committed checkpoint, while the previous recoverable checkpoint remains available. This is a hypothesis, not a reported crash test.
What makes a shard key “epoch-scoped”?

Its identity includes the worker epoch to which the shard contribution belongs. Thus a shard from an earlier epoch remains distinguishable from one associated with the replacement worker’s epoch, even if both refer to a similar portion of training state. The hypothesis does not specify the key format or how epochs are assigned.
Would the shard’s training-step ID serve the same purpose?

No. A training-step ID identifies the logical state the shard claims to represent; a worker epoch identifies the generation under which it was contributed. Two shards could claim the same step yet belong to different worker epochs. This hypothesis needs the latter distinction to address uploads arriving after replacement.
Does a late upload have to be physically prevented from reaching object storage?

Not necessarily. “Reject” can mean that a late old-epoch shard is refused as a contribution to the replacement worker’s committed manifest. The bytes might arrive, but arrival alone must not authorize their use in that checkpoint. Whether an implementation also stops the transfer or cleans up stored bytes is not specified.
Where does compare-and-swap enter the picture?

It applies at the manifest-commit boundary: a proposed manifest update succeeds only if the expected commit condition still holds. Together with checking which epoch’s shards are eligible, that is intended to prevent stale activity from committing over a newer decision or admitting old-epoch shards to the replacement worker’s checkpoint. The hypothesis does not define the exact value compared or the storage primitive used.
Could compare-and-swap by itself tell whether a shard came from a stale worker?

No. Compare-and-swap controls a conditional change to the manifest. Epoch-scoped shard keys provide the distinction needed to recognize which worker generation a shard belongs to. An atomic conditional commit would not make an ineligible shard eligible merely because its proposed manifest update happened to be atomic.
Could epoch-scoped keys by themselves protect the manifest?

They identify different epochs, but identification alone does not enforce which candidate is allowed to commit. The hypothesis pairs them with compare-and-swap manifest commits so stale or competing commit attempts cannot simply replace the selected manifest without satisfying the expected condition. Whether the pairing works under an actual worker replacement remains to be evaluated.
What exactly is the “previous recoverable checkpoint” in the prediction?

It is an already committed checkpoint eligible for restore before the candidate affected by the worker replacement. Preserving it means that an unsuccessful, stale, or incomplete new commit must not destroy that recovery option. The hypothesis does not specify its training step, the number of older checkpoints retained, or a retention period.
Is preserving the previous checkpoint the same as completing the interrupted upload?

No. The interrupted candidate may remain incomplete and never become committed. The prediction is that late uploads cannot compromise the manifest commit and that the previously recoverable checkpoint remains available. It does not promise to finish the candidate that was being uploaded when the worker was replaced.
If the late shard passes checksum verification, would that override its stale epoch?

No. A checksum addresses integrity of the shard’s bytes; it does not establish eligibility for a replacement worker’s manifest. The hypothesis calls for rejecting a late old-epoch upload as a contribution even if its bytes are intact. Integrity and epoch eligibility are separate conditions.
Suppose its global index is exactly the one the new manifest is missing. Can we include it?

A matching global index identifies the portion the shard represents, but it does not remove the epoch distinction. The proposed rule is meant to prevent a late old-epoch shard from entering the replacement worker’s committed manifest solely because it fills a missing position. The candidate still needs an eligible, complete, consistent set of shards to commit.
Does the hypothesis say a replacement worker must immediately create a new checkpoint?

No. It concerns what happens to late uploads and manifest commits after worker replacement, and whether the previous recoverable checkpoint is preserved. It does not give a deadline for a new checkpoint, say that the interrupted candidate can be completed, or specify how the replacement worker captures state.
If a compare-and-swap attempt fails, does that make the previous checkpoint corrupt?

It should not under the predicted behavior. A failed conditional attempt would not be a successful manifest commit, and preserving the previous recoverable checkpoint is an explicit part of the hypothesis. We cannot claim that a particular implementation achieves this without observing it, and the hypothesis does not specify how failed attempts are handled afterward.
Could a successful compare-and-swap still commit a mixed-step checkpoint?

Yes, unless eligibility and consistency are checked as well. Compare-and-swap only governs the conditional manifest change; it cannot establish that every model, optimizer, and RNG shard represents the same logical step. A complete, matching candidate remains necessary for a globally consistent checkpoint. This hypothesis specifically addresses stale uploads after replacement and preservation of the previous recovery option.
Does the previous checkpoint have to be stored separately from any uncommitted shards?

The prediction requires that later unfinished or rejected checkpoint work not invalidate the previous recoverable checkpoint. It does not prescribe a storage layout or a physical separation scheme. The important distinction is between the already committed recovery state and shards or manifest attempts belonging to an in-progress candidate.
What if an old worker resumes activity after the replacement starts?

Its activity would still be associated with the old worker epoch under the proposed key scheme. The intended fencing behavior is that those contributions cannot be accepted into the replacement worker’s committed manifest. The hypothesis does not specify how the old worker is stopped or whether it can continue sending bytes.
Would one successful replacement scenario prove the claim for any single-worker crash?

No. It would provide an observation for that scenario. The broader goal requires recovery of a committed, globally consistent model, optimizer, and RNG state after any single-worker crash; this hypothesis predicts protection against late uploads following worker replacement and preservation of a previous recoverable checkpoint. It does not itself report general crash-recovery coverage.
What observations would bear directly on the two predictions?

One would check whether a late old-epoch upload is rejected from the replacement worker’s committed manifest. The other would check whether the previously committed checkpoint remains selectable and recoverable after the attempted new commit. Observing only the late upload’s arrival, or only a failed compare-and-swap, would not establish both outcomes.
Does this hypothesis include a TP=8-to-TP=2 or other cross-layout restore?

No. Its focus is shard and manifest eligibility across worker epochs. Restoring model and optimizer tensors under a different tensor-parallel degree and remapping logical RNG streams are separate cross-layout responsibilities. Preserving a recoverable checkpoint here does not, by itself, demonstrate a particular cross-layout restore.
And does it predict checkpoint-induced throughput loss within 5%?

No throughput outcome is stated in this hypothesis. The broader design still has the limit of 5% loss versus checkpoint-free training, and epoch-scoped keys or conditional commits could have costs. We should not claim that this proposal meets that limit without a throughput comparison.
How would you state the hypothesis succinctly without treating the safeguards as already verified?

We hypothesize that epoch-scoped shard keys and compare-and-swap manifest commits will exclude late old-epoch uploads after worker replacement from the replacement worker’s committed checkpoint, while preserving the previous recoverable checkpoint. Whether they achieve both outcomes remains to be tested.

Let’s test the worker-replacement hypothesis: crash one uploader mid-checkpoint, replace its epoch, release its delayed uploads, and verify both manifest fencing and restoration from the previous checkpoint.

That exercise targets the race between an interrupted upload and a replacement worker epoch. The sequence matters: crash one uploader while the checkpoint is in progress, replace its epoch, then allow the delayed uploads to arrive. Check whether those old-epoch shards are excluded from any manifest committed for the replacement epoch, and separately check that the previous committed checkpoint can still be restored. These are planned checks, not reported outcomes.
Why release the delayed uploads after replacing the epoch?

That ordering puts the old uploader’s in-flight work in contact with the new epoch. If the uploads arrive only before replacement, they do not exercise the same stale-contribution question. Releasing them afterward tests whether arrival alone can cause an old-epoch shard to enter a replacement worker’s committed manifest.
Do we need to crash all the workers to exercise this?

No. The stated activity crashes one uploader mid-checkpoint. It does not call for a multiple-worker failure. The test is focused on how the system handles that uploader’s delayed shards after its epoch is replaced.
Does “mid-checkpoint” mean the checkpoint must already be committed when the uploader crashes?

No. It places the crash during checkpoint work, before the interrupted candidate can simply be assumed complete and committed. That makes the delayed-upload race meaningful. The activity does not specify exactly how much of the candidate has uploaded at the crash point.
What does it mean to replace the uploader’s epoch rather than merely restart its process?

For this test, replacement must establish a distinguishable current worker epoch so the crashed uploader’s contributions can be identified as belonging to the old one. The hypothesis uses epoch-scoped shard keys for that distinction. The activity does not prescribe how a replacement process starts or how the epoch value is assigned.
If the old uploads eventually appear in object storage, has fencing already failed?

Not necessarily. Persisting bytes and accepting them into a committed manifest are different events. The manifest-fencing check concerns whether old-epoch uploads can become eligible members of the replacement worker’s committed checkpoint. They may arrive as delayed uploads without being authorized for that commit.
So what should we inspect to verify manifest fencing?

Inspect the commit outcome and the shards the committed manifest, if any, references. The relevant question is whether a shard from the crashed uploader’s stale epoch appears in a manifest committed for the replacement epoch. A completed upload by itself does not answer that question, nor does the existence of a manifest without checking which contributions it authorizes.
Do epoch-scoped shard keys alone establish that the manifest rejected the old shards?

No. They let the old and replacement epochs be distinguished. Verification still has to establish that the commit decision respected that distinction. A key can accurately identify a stale shard while an erroneous manifest still references it.
Where does the compare-and-swap part of the hypothesis show up in this test?

It is relevant to how a candidate manifest becomes committed after replacement. The activity can check whether the conditional commit boundary prevents stale activity from changing the committed recovery state. The test description does not prescribe the expected compare value, the number of commit attempts, or a particular outcome for an individual attempt.
If a compare-and-swap attempt fails, can we call that proof of fencing?

Not by itself. A failed attempt might indicate that a conditional update was not applied, but the stated property is that delayed old-epoch shards do not enter the replacement worker’s committed manifest. Verifying that property requires looking at the resulting commit eligibility or manifest membership, not inferring it solely from one operation’s return value.
Could a late shard have the same global index and training-step ID as a shard the replacement needs?

That possibility is precisely why the epoch distinction matters. A global index identifies a shard’s place in the checkpoint, and a step ID identifies the logical training step it claims; neither alone establishes that a contribution belongs to the current worker epoch. The test should check whether the stale shard is excluded even if other identifiers would make it look relevant.
Should we make its checksum fail so the system will reject it?

The stated test is about epoch fencing, not corrupt-shard detection. A checksum failure would raise a separate integrity issue and would not show that an otherwise intact stale-epoch shard is excluded for the right eligibility reason. The activity does not specify altering any checksum.
What if the delayed uploads are accepted into a provisional set but never appear in a committed manifest?

Those are distinct observations. The manifest-fencing requirement concerns the committed recovery boundary: provisional receipt does not make the shards part of a recoverable checkpoint. The test should avoid calling mere receipt a committed stale-shard inclusion, while still checking that no later commit admits those contributions.
Does fencing require that the interrupted candidate be completed by the replacement worker?

No. The activity tests exclusion of stale contributions and restoration from the previous checkpoint. It does not require the replacement worker to complete the interrupted candidate. If the candidate cannot be made complete with eligible shards, it should not be treated as committed merely to keep checkpoint progress moving.
Why verify the previous-checkpoint restore separately?

Excluding a late shard addresses one half of the hypothesis; preserving a usable recovery point addresses the other. A system might refuse the old uploads yet still mishandle its previously committed manifest. Actually restoring the previous checkpoint tests whether that recovery option remains usable after the crash, epoch replacement, and delayed-upload release.
What is meant by the previous checkpoint here?

It is the committed, recoverable checkpoint that precedes the interrupted checkpoint candidate. The test does not identify its training-step number or how many earlier checkpoints exist. It is distinct from the in-progress candidate whose uploader crashes.
Would finding the previous manifest in storage be enough to verify restore?

No. Manifest presence is weaker than restoration. The activity explicitly calls for a previous-checkpoint restore, so the check should establish that the committed checkpoint can actually be used to reconstruct its required training state. Simply finding a manifest would not show that its necessary shards can be read and used.
Does that recovered state have to include optimizer and RNG, or is loading the model sufficient for this exercise?

The recoverable checkpoint in the broader design represents model, optimizer, and RNG state. A model-only load would not establish restoration of the previous training checkpoint as required. The activity does not specify a numerical comparison of each component, but calling the restore successful should not omit the optimizer or RNG portions.
Does the test require a restore under a different tensor-parallel degree?

No tensor-parallel change is specified for this activity. Its focus is the single-uploader crash, epoch replacement, late uploads, manifest fencing, and restoration of the previous checkpoint. A successful result here would not, by itself, be a cross-layout restore result.
If the previous checkpoint restores, does that prove the interrupted checkpoint was also recoverable?

No. The previous checkpoint is already committed; the interrupted candidate is separate. Restoring the former shows that the recovery option survived the replacement scenario. It does not imply that shards still in flight at the crash formed a complete, committed checkpoint.
Could the system legitimately leave the interrupted candidate uncommitted throughout the test?

Yes. The test does not require that candidate to commit. The proposed safety rule is to prevent stale shards from entering a replacement worker’s committed manifest and retain the previous recoverable checkpoint. An incomplete or ineligible candidate should not be promoted to committed status solely because its upload was interrupted.
How do we distinguish a stale upload rejected by epoch fencing from a shard that was simply missing?

The test sequence releases the delayed uploads after epoch replacement, giving an opportunity to observe their arrival and the subsequent eligibility decision. To verify fencing, the observation needs to connect the old-epoch shard to its exclusion from the committed manifest. If no delayed upload arrived, absence from the manifest alone would be a weaker test of the stated race.
Do we need to assert that every delayed upload gets deleted?

No source or target tensor-parallel degree is specified. The restore check concerns the latest recoverable checkpoint after worker-replacement races. Cross-layout resharding of model and optimizer tensors and remapping of logical RNG state are separate requirements, not measured outcomes of this activity as written.
Can the replay establish the 5% checkpoint-induced throughput limit?

No training-throughput comparison is specified. The 5% limit is relative to checkpoint-free training, whereas this activity measures stale commits and whether the latest checkpoint restores. Correctness of the transaction cannot stand in for a throughput measurement.
What would a precise report keep separate if the replay is carried out?

It should identify which epoch-reuse, delayed-upload, and unchanged-HEAD conditions were exercised; report stale manifest commit outcomes under transactional incarnation UUID-and-HEAD validation; and report separately whether the latest eligible checkpoint was restored. It should not conflate upload arrival with commitment, commit rejection with restoration, or the restore result with an unmeasured throughput figure.
Can you restate the activity concisely without implying it has passed?

Replay epoch-reuse, delayed-upload, and unchanged-HEAD worker-replacement races with transactional validation of nonreusable worker-incarnation UUIDs and HEAD. Measure stale manifest commits and test restoration of the latest eligible checkpoint; no outcome is supplied yet.
What did the incarnation-UUID replay report across the worker-replacement races?

Across 500 replayed races, incarnation UUID validation rejected every stale manifest. All restores selected the latest complete checkpoint. Those are the reported outcomes for the replay; the finding does not give a separate count of stale manifest attempts or restores.
Were the epoch-reuse, delayed-upload, and unchanged-HEAD conditions part of those replays?

Yes. Those are the race conditions the evaluation set out to replay with transactional incarnation UUID validation. The result gives an aggregate outcome across 500 replayed races, rather than a separate result for each condition.
Can I say there were exactly 500 stale manifests and all 500 were rejected?

No. The number 500 counts replayed races, not stale manifests. The evidence says every stale manifest encountered in those races was rejected, but it does not state how many stale manifest attempts there were.
Does “every stale manifest” mean every manifest attempt was rejected?
No. The finding concerns manifests identified as stale. It does not say that all manifest attempts were stale, or report the outcomes of non-stale attempts.
And does “all restores” mean there was exactly one restore per race?

That count is not specified. The finding says all restores selected the latest complete checkpoint, but it does not give the number of restore attempts or say how they were distributed across the 500 races.
What should I say about numeric epoch reuse specifically?

You can identify epoch reuse as one of the replayed race conditions and report that, across the stated replays, incarnation UUID validation rejected every stale manifest. The evidence does not give a separate epoch-reuse count or a condition-specific rejection rate.
Does the finding explain how the UUID validation was implemented?

No. The evaluation concerns transactional worker-incarnation UUID validation, but the result does not describe the UUID format, membership representation, transaction internals, or the exact check applied to each shard and manifest.
Can we conclude that the late uploads never arrived?

No. Delayed uploads are among the replayed conditions, but the observation is about rejecting stale manifests. A shard can arrive without becoming part of an accepted manifest. The finding does not report upload completion or cancellation counts.
What if a delayed shard remained in object storage?

That would be a separate storage observation, and none is supplied here. The reported rejection concerns stale manifests, not deletion of old shards or prevention of their bytes from reaching storage.
Does rejection tell us the stale shards failed checksum verification?
No checksum results are reported. Worker-incarnation eligibility and shard-byte integrity are distinct properties. We should not attribute the stale-manifest rejections to checksum failures.
How should I interpret “latest complete checkpoint”?

It identifies the most recent checkpoint considered complete for the restore selection, rather than the newest upload or most recent manifest attempt. The finding reports that every restore selected that checkpoint. It does not provide its training-step ID, creation time, or age.
Is that necessarily the checkpoint being assembled when a worker was replaced?

Not necessarily. An in-progress candidate is not automatically a complete checkpoint. The evidence identifies the selected checkpoint by its status as the latest complete one; it does not say whether it was the candidate active at replacement or an earlier checkpoint.
Can I report that every restore successfully recovered model, optimizer, and RNG values?

The precise finding is that all restores *selected* the latest complete checkpoint. It does not supply component-by-component recovery results or comparisons of model, optimizer, and RNG values. Selection should not be expanded into those additional measurements.
Does it establish that no incomplete checkpoint was selected?

For the restores reported here, yes: each selected the latest *complete* checkpoint. That observation is scoped to these replays. It does not describe every possible restore outside them or provide an audit of how completeness was determined.
Were any stale manifests selected for restore?

The report says every stale manifest was rejected and all restores selected the latest complete checkpoint. It does not give a separate manifest-by-manifest restore log, but it does not report selection of a stale manifest.
Can the 500 races be described as proof for every possible worker failure?
No. They establish the stated outcomes across the 500 replayed races under the conditions evaluated. They do not enumerate every worker-failure timing, system configuration, or future race.
Did the replay measure whether the selected checkpoint was only a few steps old?

No checkpoint-age value is supplied. “Latest complete” identifies which eligible checkpoint was selected; it does not quantify the gap between that checkpoint and the point of worker replacement or restore.
What about the 5% throughput-loss target?

This finding reports stale-manifest rejection and checkpoint selection, not throughput. It gives no tokens-per-second comparison with checkpoint-free training, so it cannot establish the checkpoint-induced throughput-loss percentage.
Does selecting the latest complete checkpoint show that it restored under a different tensor-parallel layout?

No tensor-parallel source or target degree is reported for these restores. The observation concerns selection after worker-replacement races, not resharding model and optimizer state or remapping logical RNG streams across layouts.
Would it be accurate to say that transactional incarnation UUID validation rejected stale manifests even when HEAD did not change?

The unchanged-HEAD race was included in the replay activity, and the aggregate result says every stale manifest was rejected across the replays. You can state those facts together, but the evidence does not provide a separate count or transaction trace for unchanged-HEAD cases.
How do I avoid making the result sound like every upload was rejected?

Name the committed-boundary object precisely: stale *manifests* were rejected. Do not substitute “uploads” or “shards.” Then state separately that the restores selected the latest complete checkpoint.
Give me a concise report that preserves the denominator and the scope of both outcomes.

Across 500 replayed worker-replacement races covering epoch reuse, delayed uploads, and unchanged HEAD, incarnation UUID validation rejected every stale manifest; all restores selected the latest complete checkpoint. The finding does not provide counts of individual manifest attempts or restores.

I want an integrated benchmark: run 20,000 steps with incarnation-fenced TP=8→2 restores under crashes, corrupt shards, ragged attention, and upload stalls. Measure training-state consistency and throughput loss.

That brings the failure, restore, and performance questions into one 20,000-step benchmark. It calls for evaluating whether an incarnation-fenced checkpoint remains a consistent source for TP=8→2 restoration under the named conditions, and for measuring checkpoint-induced throughput loss. It is a benchmark plan, not a report that the restores succeed or that throughput meets the design target.
What does TP=8→2 specify here?

It specifies the cross-layout restore: the checkpointed state originates under tensor-parallel degree 8 and is restored under tensor-parallel degree 2. The consistency measurement should concern the training state reconstructed after that change, rather than merely whether a manifest can be opened. The plan does not specify a particular tensor placement or number of restore attempts.
Does 20,000 steps mean 20,000 restores?

No. It gives the benchmark’s step scope. The activity does not specify how many checkpoints or restores occur during those steps, or a checkpoint interval. We should not infer a restore count from the training-step count.
What does ‘incarnation-fenced’ add to this benchmark?

It says worker-incarnation identity is part of protecting checkpoint eligibility when workers are replaced. In this benchmark, the relevant consistency question includes whether a restore selects an eligible committed checkpoint rather than a stale worker’s manifest. The phrase does not, on its own, establish that fencing works during every crash in the run.
Does fencing mean that delayed shards cannot finish uploading?

Not necessarily. A delayed shard can be present without being eligible for a committed manifest. Incarnation fencing concerns whether a contribution from an outdated worker instance can affect the checkpoint chosen for recovery. Upload completion and checkpoint commitment should be kept distinct when interpreting the benchmark.
And what exactly would count as consistent training state?

For the checkpointing goal, it is a committed, globally consistent model, optimizer, and RNG state. After a TP=8→2 restore, those components must still correspond to one recoverable training state, rather than being drawn from incompatible checkpoint candidates or logical steps. Checking that a restore process starts would be weaker than assessing the state it reconstructs.
Can we check only the model weights to keep the benchmark simple?

Not if the result is meant to establish training-state consistency. The optimizer and RNG state are expressly part of the recovery requirement. A model-only check could provide information about model restoration, but it would not answer the full consistency question named for this activity.
Does global consistency require identical values on every rank at TP=2?

No. Different ranks can hold different portions of a distributed state. The question is whether their portions, taken together, reconstruct the model, optimizer, and logical RNG state of one committed checkpoint. Agreement on a logical state does not mean every physical rank contains the same tensor values.
Is matching step IDs sufficient for that conclusion?

Matching step IDs would be relevant evidence of alignment, but matching labels alone cannot prove that each shard contains the corresponding state or that the complete checkpoint was restored. State consistency is broader than an ID comparison, particularly when the benchmark includes corrupt shards and a change in tensor-parallel degree.
How do corrupt shards fit into a restore from a committed manifest?

They test the distinction between a manifest being committed and the required shard bytes being usable. The proposed persistence path calls for checksum-verified shards in durable object storage. A corrupt required shard must not be silently treated as valid merely because a manifest references it. The benchmark does not specify when corruption occurs, how many shards are affected, or what recovery path is available in each case.
Should we assume every corrupted shard can be repaired?

No repair capability is specified. The consistency criterion is that corrupted state must not be passed off as a valid, globally consistent restore. Whether another complete checkpoint remains available, or a given restore can proceed after corruption, must be observed rather than assumed.
If a checksum detects corruption, is the recovery requirement automatically met?

No. Detection prevents one kind of invalid state from being accepted, but recovery also requires a committed, usable checkpoint containing the model, optimizer, and RNG state. Detecting that a required shard is corrupt does not itself reconstruct the missing valid data. Detection and successful restore are separate possible observations.
What should a crash challenge in the integrated benchmark?

It challenges whether checkpoint selection and restoration remain sound when a worker fails and incarnation membership can change. A candidate still being uploaded at the crash cannot be assumed committed. The consistency measurement should distinguish an eligible complete checkpoint from incomplete or stale work, and assess what is actually restored. The plan does not prescribe crash timing, the identities of failed workers, or the number of crashes.
Can we claim this benchmarks every possible single-worker crash?

Not from the activity description alone. The broader goal requires recovery after any single-worker crash, but this plan simply specifies crashes as a benchmark condition. The coverage of worker identities and crash timings would have to be stated and observed before making an exhaustive claim.
What does ragged attention contribute? Is it another worker-failure case?

No. Ragged attention exercises the cross-layout computation, particularly whether the restored logical RNG state remains coherent when attention work is tiled unevenly. It is a different condition from a worker crash. The activity does not specify particular tile sizes or mandate a separate bitwise-mask comparison.
So should we say this benchmark necessarily measures fused-attention masks bitwise?

Not on the stated activity alone. It says to measure state consistency and throughput loss under ragged attention; it does not explicitly name a mask-level measurement or an update-error threshold for this benchmark. Such observations could clarify RNG behavior if specified, but should not be reported as though this activity already included or produced them.
Could a restore have matching attention behavior and still have the wrong optimizer state?

Yes. An RNG-related observation would address only one part of the training state. The TP=8→2 restore still has to reconstruct optimizer state consistently with the model. No single attention observation should substitute for assessing the full model, optimizer, and RNG recovery requirement.
Where do upload stalls matter if uploads are asynchronous?

Asynchronous work can still be delayed. Upload stalls can affect when a candidate has all required shards and is eligible for atomic manifest commitment; they can also affect training throughput. The benchmark is intended to measure behavior under those stalls, without assuming that asynchrony makes their effects disappear.
If uploads stall, can a manifest be committed using just the shards that arrived?

Not as a complete checkpoint if required shards are missing. The proposed recovery boundary permits restores only from complete, atomically committed manifests. A stalled upload may leave a candidate pending; it must not turn a partial model, optimizer, or RNG state into a recoverable checkpoint.
Does this activity say the crashes, corruption, ragged attention, and stalls all occur at once?

It names all four benchmark conditions but does not specify their scheduling or whether every one is present in every run. A report should say which conditions were actually exercised together and which were exercised separately. We should not invent a sequence or interaction pattern from the list.
Would measuring each condition separately answer how they interact?

Separate observations would describe each tested condition, but would not automatically establish behavior when conditions overlap. Conversely, an aggregate result under overlapping conditions might not isolate an individual cause. The activity leaves the schedule open, so its eventual conclusions should reflect the combinations actually evaluated.
What is the throughput baseline for the loss measurement?

The design’s performance target compares checkpointed training with checkpoint-free training. Checkpoint-induced throughput loss must be no more than 5% versus that baseline. The benchmark calls for measuring throughput loss, but does not supply tokens-per-second values or a measured percentage.
If throughput loss were 5% exactly, would that satisfy the target?

Yes. The target is a loss of *at most* 5% relative to checkpoint-free training, so 5% is the boundary; more than 5% would exceed it. That is an interpretation of the target, not an observed result for the 20,000-step benchmark.
Could we calculate the loss just from how long an upload stall lasts?

No. A stall duration is not a throughput measurement. Its effect depends on how it interacts with training, capture, storage, and checkpoint commitment. To assess the 5% target, the checkpointing run’s training throughput must be compared with checkpoint-free training on a like-for-like basis.
Should time spent restoring after a crash be silently reported as checkpoint-induced training-throughput loss?

The activity does not define its throughput-accounting method. It should state how the throughput comparison treats crash and restore periods rather than silently changing the denominator or presenting a restore delay as though it were a measured training-throughput loss. State consistency and the throughput comparison should be reported distinctly.
Does a good throughput figure prove the corrupted-shard case was handled correctly?

No. A throughput figure addresses performance, not whether corrupted required shards were detected or a consistent checkpoint was recovered. Likewise, sound corruption handling would not, by itself, establish a ≤5% throughput loss. Both kinds of evidence are needed for this integrated benchmark.
Would one successful restore prove that all committed manifests in the 20,000-step run are sound?

No. A restore demonstrates behavior for the selected checkpoint under the tested conditions. It does not automatically audit every manifest candidate or every committed checkpoint in the benchmark. Any reported consistency conclusion should state which restores and checkpoints were examined.
Can the latest available shard set be the recovery point if its manifest has not committed?

No. Shard recency does not make a checkpoint eligible for recovery. The recovery point must be a complete, atomically committed manifest with usable required shards. If the newest candidate is unfinished or ineligible after a crash or upload stall, it should not be substituted for a valid committed checkpoint.
Does selecting a committed manifest prove its shards are uncorrupted?

No. Commitment and checksum verification answer different questions. The corrupt-shard condition makes it important to assess whether the required bytes pass integrity checks and can reconstruct the stated training state. A manifest’s committed status cannot turn corrupt bytes into valid model, optimizer, or RNG state.
How is incarnation fencing different from checking shard checksums?

Incarnation fencing addresses whether a worker’s contribution remains eligible after replacement. Checksum verification addresses whether stored shard bytes match their expected integrity values. An old worker’s shard could be intact but ineligible, while a current worker’s shard could be eligible by incarnation but corrupt. The benchmark brings both concerns together without making either check a substitute for the other.
Does this benchmark, as phrased, already establish that TP=8→2 restoration preserves every subsequent update?

No. It specifies a TP=8→2 restore and measurements of state consistency and throughput loss. It does not report any outcome, define a numerical update-error metric, or promise agreement for all subsequent training steps. Cross-layout correctness must be assessed within whatever comparisons the benchmark actually performs.
Could I describe the activity as simply rerunning a throughput benchmark with more failures?

That would omit much of its stated scope. It is an integrated 20,000-step benchmark of incarnation-fenced TP=8→2 restores under crashes, corrupt shards, ragged attention, and upload stalls. It asks for *both* training-state consistency and throughput loss, rather than only a performance number.
What should the final benchmark report keep separate?

It should distinguish the conditions exercised, which complete committed checkpoint each restore used, what was observed about model, optimizer, and RNG consistency, and the measured throughput loss versus checkpoint-free training. It should not turn a rejected stale manifest into a successful restore, a detected corrupt shard into recovered data, or a restore observation into an unmeasured throughput result.
Can you state the planned activity succinctly without implying any results?

Benchmark 20,000 steps of incarnation-fenced TP=8→2 checkpoint restoration under crashes, corrupt shards, ragged attention, and upload stalls. Measure whether restores recover a committed, globally consistent model, optimizer, and RNG state, and measure checkpoint-induced throughput loss against checkpoint-free training and the 5% limit. The activity specifies no outcomes.
What did the integrated TP=8→2 benchmark report?

Across 100 single-worker crashes, the TP=8→2 restores recovered consistent model, optimizer, and RNG states. Corrupt shards were rejected, and training throughput dropped 4.9% versus checkpoint-free training. Those are the reported recovery, integrity, and performance observations.
Does the recovery observation include the optimizer and RNG state, or just the model?
It explicitly includes all three: model, optimizer, and RNG state. Describing the result as a model-only restore would omit two components that the benchmark reports as consistent.
What does TP=8→2 identify in that result?

It identifies the tensor-parallel layout change: the checkpointed state came from TP=8 and was restored at TP=2. The reported consistency observation applies to those cross-layout restores, not to every possible pair of tensor-parallel degrees.
Were the 100 failures simultaneous?
No. The result describes 100 single-worker crashes. It does not report simultaneous crashes of multiple workers or establish an outcome for that different failure condition.
Can I say the benchmark proved recovery after every possible single-worker crash?

The precise observation is recovery of consistent model, optimizer, and RNG states across the 100 single-worker crashes tested. The finding does not enumerate every possible crash timing, worker identity, or system configuration, so it should not be expanded beyond those tested cases.
Do we know which training step each restore recovered?

No step IDs are given in this finding. It reports consistency of the recovered training-state components, but not the step number of any selected checkpoint or the amount of progress between a crash and its restore.
Does “consistent” mean every TP=2 rank held identical model and optimizer values?

No. A distributed restore can place different portions of state on different ranks. The reported property is that the recovered model, optimizer, and RNG states were consistent as a training state. It does not say every rank contained numerically identical values.
Is that stronger than reporting matching step-ID labels?

The finding reports recovery of consistent model, optimizer, and RNG states, rather than merely listing matching step IDs. It does not, however, supply a component-by-component numerical comparison or explain the consistency-check procedure. We should preserve the reported conclusion without inventing its measurement details.
What exactly happened to the corrupt shards?
They were rejected. The result does not state how many were corrupt, whether they held model, optimizer, or RNG data, when corruption was detected, or whether their bytes were deleted afterward.
Does rejecting a corrupt shard mean the system repaired that shard?
No repair is reported. Rejection means the corrupt shard was not accepted as valid checkpoint data. We should not infer a repair method or claim that the rejected bytes were reconstructed.
Can we tell which checkpoint was used when a corrupt shard was rejected?

Not from this finding. It reports both corrupt-shard rejection and consistent TP=8→2 restores across the tested crashes, but does not identify the manifest or checkpoint selected in each corruption case. It would be an added detail to describe a particular fallback or selection sequence.
Does the result give a count of corrupt-shard incidents?
No. The number 100 counts single-worker crashes, not corrupt shards. The finding reports that corrupt shards were rejected without giving a shard count or a rejection rate.
Was a stale worker manifest accepted during these restores?

This finding does not provide a stale-manifest count or a manifest-by-manifest record. It reports consistent restored states, corrupt-shard rejection, and throughput loss. We should not add a separate assertion about every commit decision during the benchmark.
Can we say that each restore came from an atomically committed manifest?

The benchmark concerns a checkpointing design that restores committed state, but this evidence does not list individual manifest commits or their atomicity checks. Its direct reported outcome is that TP=8→2 restores recovered consistent model, optimizer, and RNG states across 100 single-worker crashes. It is better not to turn that into an unstated per-manifest audit.
The run involved ragged attention. Does this result give a bitwise mask comparison for it?

No bitwise mask measurement is stated in this finding. Ragged attention was among the benchmark conditions, but the reported outcomes are recovered training-state consistency, corrupt-shard rejection, and the 4.9% throughput decrease. A specific mask-agreement claim would require a separately reported observation.
Do we know whether upload stalls happened during every crash?

No schedule is given. Upload stalls were among the benchmark conditions, but the result does not say whether a stall overlapped each of the 100 crashes or how the conditions were distributed. It would be too specific to attribute an individual recovery to a particular overlap.
Could I attribute the 4.9% slowdown to the corrupt-shard checks?

No. The 4.9% figure is the reported throughput drop versus checkpoint-free training for the benchmark. It does not break out the costs of checksum verification, incarnation fencing, uploads, or any other checkpoint-related activity.
Is 4.9% a restore-error rate?
No. It is a training-throughput decrease relative to checkpoint-free training. It is not a percentage of failed restores, corrupt shards, or differing RNG values.
Can we calculate the tokens per second from that percentage?
Not without an absolute throughput value for at least one side of the comparison. The finding gives the relative decrease—4.9% versus checkpoint-free training—but no tokens-per-second figures.
Does the result say whether the throughput comparison includes crash-recovery downtime?

It does not specify how the throughput measurement accounts for crash and restore periods. We can report the stated 4.9% drop and its checkpoint-free baseline, but should not add an accounting convention that is not given.
Is 4.9% the slowdown for each individual restore?

No per-restore throughput figures are reported. The 4.9% value describes the benchmark's throughput comparison with checkpoint-free training; it should not be assigned separately to each of the 100 crash cases.
Does the 20,000-step benchmark description let us infer how many checkpoints committed?

No. The benchmark ran for 20,000 steps, but this finding does not provide a checkpoint count, a commit count, or a checkpoint interval. The 100 single-worker crashes likewise should not be treated as a count of committed checkpoints.
Could a corrupt shard be rejected while the restore still recovers a consistent state?

The finding reports both outcomes in the integrated evaluation. It does not explain their precise sequence or specify how recovery proceeded in any case involving corruption. We can state that corrupt shards were rejected and that the reported TP=8→2 restores recovered consistent model, optimizer, and RNG states without inventing a repair or fallback mechanism.
Does the result establish bitwise equality of model and optimizer state with a TP=8 reference?

No bitwise model- or optimizer-state comparison is specified. The observation is recovery of consistent state after the TP=8→2 layout change. Consistency should not be silently strengthened into bitwise equality of every tensor value with a separately measured reference.
Can you give me one sentence that retains the crash count, cross-layout condition, shard result, and throughput baseline?
Across 100 single-worker crashes, TP=8→2 restores recovered consistent model, optimizer, and RNG states; corrupt shards were rejected, and throughput dropped 4.9% versus checkpoint-free training.

Using the recovered states from the TP=8→2 benchmark, let’s crash the coordinator immediately before and immediately after HEAD commit. In each case, compare visible manifest completeness and the model, optimizer, and RNG hashes.

That isolates the coordinator crash relative to the HEAD commit boundary. The proposed observations are which manifest, if any, is visible and complete on each side of that boundary, and whether the recovered model, optimizer, and RNG hashes correspond to the checkpoint selected for restore. This is a further test using those recovered states, not a reported result of the coordinator-crash experiment.
Why test both sides of HEAD commit?

They distinguish a candidate whose HEAD commit has not happened from one whose commit has happened before the coordinator crashes. The question is whether the recovery-visible checkpoint changes cleanly at that boundary, without making an incomplete candidate appear committed or losing the state associated with a completed commit. The activity does not tell us what either crash will reveal.
Does a crash before HEAD commit necessarily mean no checkpoint can be restored?

No. It means the candidate awaiting that commit should not be assumed to have become the new recovery point. A previously committed checkpoint may still be eligible. The test must observe what is visible and what state can be recovered rather than infer that there is no recovery option.
What about a crash after HEAD commit? Can we assume the new state is recoverable?

That is what the post-commit case is intended to examine, not an outcome to assume. The test should check that the manifest made visible by HEAD is complete and that recovery yields the corresponding model, optimizer, and RNG state. A completed HEAD operation alone is not a substitute for those observations.
What do you mean by a ‘visible manifest’ here?

The manifest that a recovery attempt can identify through the checkpoint-selection path after the coordinator crash. A candidate manifest or some uploaded shards might exist without being the manifest selected through HEAD. The activity asks to compare what is visible, not merely what objects are present in storage.
Could a manifest object exist before HEAD commit?

Possibly; the activity does not prescribe the order in which objects are written. But the existence of an object would not, by itself, make that candidate the committed recovery point. The observation of interest is whether recovery visibility respects the HEAD commit boundary and whether the visible manifest is complete.
How should we interpret manifest completeness?

A complete manifest must identify the required pieces of one checkpointed training state, not just whichever model or optimizer shards happened to arrive. For the recovery goal, the state includes model, optimizer, and RNG components. The activity does not specify a manifest schema, shard count, or completeness-check procedure.
Is seeing a complete manifest sufficient to call the restore consistent?

No. Completeness addresses whether all required portions are accounted for; it does not alone establish that the recovered values belong together or match the intended checkpoint. Comparing model, optimizer, and RNG hashes supplies a separate observation about the reconstructed state. Both comparisons are explicitly part of this activity.
What are the hashes being compared against?

The test should use the corresponding checkpoint state drawn from the recovered states identified for this activity. The essential point is to compare each restored component with the state the visible committed checkpoint is supposed to represent. The activity does not specify how reference hashes are recorded, what hash algorithm is used, or particular expected hash values.
Should the before-commit and after-commit restores necessarily have identical hashes?

Not necessarily. If they select different committed checkpoints, their model, optimizer, and RNG states may legitimately differ. Each case should be compared with its own selected checkpoint's expected state. Requiring the two cases to have identical hashes would add a condition the activity does not state.
Could a model hash match while the optimizer hash differs?

That would be a distinct observation and should be reported as such. The goal is a coherent training-state restore, so a model match cannot stand in for the optimizer or RNG comparisons. The activity explicitly names all three hashes to avoid treating a model-only match as sufficient.
Is the RNG hash a substitute for checking which manifest is visible?

No. A hash comparison concerns reconstructed state, while manifest visibility and completeness concern which checkpoint was eligible and what it contained. Even a matching RNG hash would not tell us that an incomplete manifest was never exposed. Conversely, a complete visible manifest would not tell us that the intended RNG state was recovered.
Does ‘before HEAD commit’ specify an exact instruction where the coordinator is killed?

No. It specifies the ordering relative to the HEAD commit. The activity does not define an instruction-level pause point or the state of every upload when the crash occurs. A report should make clear how each crash was positioned relative to commit without inventing a particular implementation sequence.
If the coordinator crashes after shards are uploaded but before HEAD commit, can we count them as a committed checkpoint?

Not merely because the shards have arrived. The proposed recovery rule selects complete, atomically committed manifests. The pre-commit crash case tests whether those shards remain provisional rather than being mistaken for a committed checkpoint. Their subsequent handling is not specified here.
And if HEAD commit occurred but the coordinator crashed before it could acknowledge success?

The relevant distinction in this activity is whether HEAD actually committed before the crash, not whether the coordinator reported an acknowledgment. The post-commit observations should establish what recovery sees and whether its manifest and state are complete. The activity does not specify an acknowledgment protocol or its outcome.
Could both cases select the same checkpoint?

That is possible depending on what actually became committed and visible, but it is not specified. The comparison should record the selected manifest in each case and assess its completeness and corresponding model, optimizer, and RNG hashes. We should not assume in advance that selection must differ.
What if HEAD points to a manifest but a required shard fails its checksum?

Then HEAD visibility would not, by itself, establish a usable complete recovery state. The proposed design uses checksum-verified shards, and an unverified required shard must not be silently accepted as valid. This activity names manifest completeness and state hashes as its comparisons; it does not say a corrupt shard is injected during either coordinator crash or specify a repair path.
Are we deliberately injecting another worker crash as part of this test?

The injected failure here is the coordinator crash, once before and once after HEAD commit. The activity uses states recovered in the earlier TP=8→2 benchmark, but does not specify an additional worker crash or a repeat of all its conditions in each coordinator-crash case.
Does this test specify another TP=8→2 restore?

It draws on the recovered states from that cross-layout benchmark and compares manifests and model, optimizer, and RNG hashes around a coordinator crash. It does not prescribe a new source and target tensor-parallel layout for each crash case. The focus is the HEAD commit boundary and the visibility and integrity of the recovery state.
What if the pre-commit case exposes an incomplete candidate as the recovery manifest?

That would be an observation concerning the visibility and completeness boundary: the candidate would appear recoverable before the intended HEAD commit despite lacking a complete checkpoint. Whether it occurs is precisely something to check. It is a conditional interpretation, not a reported finding.
What if the post-commit case has a complete visible manifest but an optimizer hash that does not match its reference?

Then the visibility and completeness observations would not establish that the intended optimizer state was restored. The model, optimizer, and RNG hash results should be kept separate so the discrepancy is not hidden by a complete manifest. No such discrepancy is reported by the activity itself.
Would matching hashes prove every possible future update is identical?

No. They would be evidence about the state components compared for the selected checkpoint, under the chosen hashing procedure. This activity does not specify a next-step update comparison or a guarantee about all future training behavior.
Can we use these coordinator-crash cases to calculate the 5% throughput-loss result?

No new throughput measurement is specified. This activity compares recovery-visible manifest completeness and model, optimizer, and RNG hashes before and after HEAD commit. It does not compare training tokens per second with checkpoint-free training, so it cannot supply a checkpoint-induced throughput-loss figure.
Does passing these two crash timings prove safety under every possible coordinator failure?

No. They examine crashes placed on either side of the HEAD commit boundary. Any conclusion should be scoped to the timings and states actually tested, rather than all possible coordinator failures or storage behavior.
How should the observations be reported if we run this?

For each crash position—before HEAD commit and after HEAD commit—identify the manifest visible for recovery, report whether it is complete, and report the model, optimizer, and RNG hash comparisons against the corresponding selected checkpoint state.
